Title: North Korea ‘s Crypto Theft Operations: DOJ Seizes $1.2 Billion and Disrupts Hacker Infrastructure
Context: Department of Justice announced two separate but connected actions against North Korea ‘s cryptocurrency theft operations
Full Text:
The DOJ seized over $1.2 billion from North Korea ‘s Binance theft, and says the same hackers are targeting open-source developers

The U.S. Department of Justice announced two separate but connected actions against North Korea ‘s cryptocurrency theft operations. The press release covers the seizure of infrastructure behind a social engineering scheme called FaceStealer and court-authorized seizures tied to the $6 billion Binance theft of October 29. Together, the two moves put more than $1.2 billion back under law enforcement control.

“Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.” states the press release published by DoJ. “These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.”

FaceStealer is the FBI’s name for a scheme North Korea-linked hackers have run for the past 18 months. The same actors go by Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff, APT38 and several other tracking names depending on who is writing the report. They’ve stolen more than $400 million that way, and they’ve also started targeting people who build and maintain open-source software, trying to reach the accounts and repositories those developers control.

The process is quite specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts they have already stolen. This makes the invitations look as if they come from someone the target knows and trusts. During the meeting, they play a recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake showing a well-known person in the cryptocurrency or Web3 industry. They use advanced AI tools to create convincing videos of influential people, making the FaceStealer scheme more effective.

The hackers then pretend there is a technical problem, such as an audio issue, and ask the target to click a link or follow instructions to fix it. This leads to the installation of malware. In several cases, the attackers waited months, or even more than a year, before stealing cryptocurrency or taking control of accounts. They also used each victim’s contact lists, social media accounts and messaging apps to identify and approach new targets.

Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos recorded from FaceStealer victims.

“The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.” continues the press release. “The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.”

The operation to seize the infrastructure was led by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The mechanics are specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts stolen from earlier victims, so the invite looks like it comes from someone the target knows. Once in the meeting, the hackers play a pre-recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake of a well-known person in crypto or Web3 to simulate trusted contacts.

“The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective.” FBI continues. “Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.”

Then they introduce a fake technical problem, such as claiming the target’s audio isn’t working, and offer a link or prompt to fix it. The fix installs malware. In several cases the hackers waited months or more than a year after the initial compromise before stealing cryptocurrency or hijacking accounts. They also used each new victim’s contact lists, social media and messaging apps to reach the next round of targets.

The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos from FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant. It also published a detailed report on the scheme’s mechanics, with best practices and steps for anyone who suspects they’ve been compromised, and created a resource page at fbi.gov/facestealer. The infrastructure seizure was led by the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

“The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”

Separately, the DOJ has been working since October 29 to freeze and recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance by North Korea’s TraderTraitor unit. Combined government and private-sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion so far, and the DOJ has court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that. The Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section called it freezing about half of the historic breach before it got beyond law enforcement reach.

TraderTraitor actors continue to launder the remaining assets through cryptocurrency bridges, mixers and exchanges. The FBI, the U.S. Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation last week issued a joint cyber alert naming the addresses the actors are using and urging cryptocurrency service providers to block any transactions involving those addresses or funds derived from them.

North Korea uses cryptocurrency theft to support its weapons programs. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) has repeatedly highlighted this link. A senior official from the department’s National Security Division said the regime uses these criminal operations to raise money for its weapons program. The DOJ also pledged to use all available legal tools to seize the stolen funds and return them to their rightful owners.

The FaceStealer campaign also shows how convincing these attacks can be. According to the FBI, the scheme can trick even experienced IT professionals and users who are well aware of cybersecurity risks.

“Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges.” concludes the press release. “For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.”

Title: In Other News: New CISA Director Nominee, Connected Car Hacking, Baker Tilly Data Breach
Context: This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help...
Full Text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights:

Ex-FBI agent’s $2.47M crypto theft compromised bureau investigations

Patrick Steven Yaroch, a former FBI counterintelligence agent, faces up to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to wire fraud and money laundering over the theft of roughly $2.47 million in cryptocurrency. Yaroch used wallet credentials stored on FBI systems to make about 100 fraudulent transfers tied to 35 investigations. He took funds from investigation subjects and adversarial nation-state actors, and the thefts compromised multiple investigations and FBI sources and methods.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Baker Tilly client data taken from supplier’s platform

US accounting giant Baker Tilly is informing clients that hackers stole personal information, including Social Security numbers, from a platform operated by one of its service providers. The intrusion dates to early September and also affects clients’ dependents, including children. The firm has not named the vendor or said how many people are impacted in total, but state regulator filings point to more than 10,000 victims in Texas alone.

OpenAI agents concealed unauthorized activity

OpenAI has revealed new details about a July incident in which five AI agents conducting cybersecurity evaluations gained root privileges in CI workloads on the company’s research clusters. The agents used credentials and scripts left by earlier agents to modify evaluation settings, repair broken targets, and access restricted information. Two agents recognized that their activity was unauthorized and omitted it from their final submissions after considering how disclosure might affect their scores.

Prompt injection chain could have backdoored OpenAI’s Codex npm package

Depi researchers have described an attack chain against OpenAI’s Codex repository that started with a prompt injection in a GitHub Actions workflow and could have led to a malicious Codex release on npm. The issue-labeling workflow passed the title and body of any new issue to the Codex agent, so an attacker could execute code in the agent’s sandbox, read tokens from a GitHub runner process’s memory via .NET debug pipes, and poison the cache of a workflow with write permissions. The final step relied on a maintainer deleting a rogue release, which would yield a token trusted by npm. OpenAI has fixed the issue and awarded an initial $1,000 bounty.

Siemens details security advisory policy and planned improvements

Siemens has published a policy document that sets out how its PSIRT deals with product vulnerabilities and what its security advisories contain. Planned improvements include an API for automated lookups of product and vulnerability data, wider coverage of flaws in third-party components, more explicit “not affected” declarations, and getting advisory data into commonly used third-party vulnerability databases.

VulnCheck: Glasswing fixes lag far behind findings

VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity says that seven months after Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, he has tracked 442 CVEs credited to the company (about 0.5% of all CVEs published this year), only two of which are known to have been exploited in the wild. Anthropic’s own ledger listed 37,966 findings as of November 2, but only 7,349 have been made public and 217 are marked as fixed, while more than 1,600 have been flagged as duplicates and 419 withdrawn.

Railway puts unauthorized spend from stolen AI keys at $740,000

Railway has released a detailed incident report on the October attack, in which a threat actor used an undiscovered flaw in its build infrastructure to partially escape isolation, obtained a copy of the company’s code repository, and then abused a misconfigured OIDC binding to reach credentials that let it decrypt customer environment variables. At most 1.85% of workspaces (roughly 100,000) could have had variables decrypted. Linked-account tokens for 1,852 users were also exposed, and unauthorized spending on stolen keys is estimated at about $740,000. Railway believes the attacker wanted AI provider keys to sell for use in distillation, and says it will cover losses that providers do not refund.

Exposed MS SQL servers hijacked to deliver cryptominer and Gh0st RAT

Fortinet has analyzed a campaign in which Go-based malware with the open source Naabu scanner built in looks for internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server instances, and a companion tool then brute-forces logins using a list of more than 2,700 passwords. After a successful login, T-SQL commands enable xp_cmdshell and download or drop a loader, which installs a Monero miner disguised as a Microsoft Edge update and a Gh0st RAT variant whose features include keylogging and data theft.

Microsoft urges weight audits after ‘Lazarus’ dormant neuron backdoor research

Microsoft researchers have described Lazarus, a technique that backdoors an LLM without any training by rewriting the weights of fewer than 10 dormant neurons, so that an agent built on the model behaves normally until a trigger (such as a date or an error message) makes it emit an attacker’s command. In a demonstration, a modified Nemotron-Terminal-8B model that was debugging a server issued a command to download and run a remote script after seeing a “Connection refused” message. Because the attack needs write access to the weights and can only be reliably detected by comparing them with the originals, Microsoft recommends verifying model provenance and auditing weights the way code is audited.

Connected cars exposed by flaws in automakers’ ForgeRock deployments

Researchers Sam Curry and Shubham Shah have disclosed weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity deployments of unnamed automakers that allowed them to take over customer accounts and send remote commands to connected vehicles, including unlocking doors and starting engines. In one chain, a WAF bypass let them reach an Apache Felix console that still accepted default admin credentials, giving them code execution on production identity servers used by two automakers, which fixed the issue roughly two hours after it was reported.

Palantir CISO LoSapio nominated to fill long-vacant CISA director post

President Donald Trump has nominated Michael LoSapio, Palantir’s CISO since September 2024, to lead CISA, which has not had a Senate-confirmed director since Jen Easterly left in January 2025, Nextgov reports. Should the Senate fail to act before this Congress adjourns, Trump would need to renominate him under an incoming Democratic majority whose members have questioned Palantir’s government work. Sean Plankey, the earlier nominee, pulled out in April following a wait of over a year.

Vanderbilt tells campus to power down devices amid attack claimed by BYOD group

US-based Vanderbilt University this week told everyone in its community to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi as its IT team worked on an active cybersecurity incident that it said could affect devices, systems and cloud-based services. The BYOD group has taken credit for the attack.

Title: FBI Says North Korean Hackers Stole Over $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls
Context: Exploit the victim's Telegram account: The attacker impersonates the victim and sends tailored messages to other contacts on their behalf, proposing a Zoom or Teams meeting...
Full Text:
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has established that threat actors tied to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK aka North Korea) have stolen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency as part of a social engineering scheme codenamed FaceStealer in the last 18 months.

As part of a coordinated set of actions announced by the U.S. government, the cloud-based infrastructure used to pull off the "hard-to-detect" campaign has been seized.

In tandem, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen by the North Korea-linked TraderTraitor actors following the hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance. The plundered digital assets are used to fund Pyongyang's illicit weapons program, the DoJ added.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman in a statement.

"North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months."

According to the Justice Department, FaceStealer relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and deepfakes to facilitate cryptocurrency theft. Some aspects of the activity dovetail with a campaign documented by Kaspersky under the name GhostCall in October 2025.

The activity is linked to a prolific North Korea-linked financially motivated threat cluster tracked as BlueNoroff, which is also known by the cryptonyms APT38, CageyChameleon, CryptoCore, DangerousPassword, Nickel Gladstone, Sapphire Sleet, Stardust Chollima, and UNC1069.

The campaign involves luring targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from stolen accounts belonging to prior victims. Targets who join the meeting have their video stream recorded, while simultaneously serving an authentic, prerecorded webcam video of a previous victim or victims known to the target to build trust.

"The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective," the DoJ said. "Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target's trust."

A few seconds into the meeting, a mock technical error is presented to the victim, claiming that they cannot be heard, and they are provided a link to address the non-existent issue. The fix is a ClickFix-style lure that's designed to install malware on the victim's workstation and steal cryptocurrency, as well as abuse the target's privileges to other computer infrastructure.

In an extensive report shared with The Hacker News in July 2026, JUMPSEC revealed how the social engineering operation is built atop a phishing kit designed to impersonate videoconferencing platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams. The cybersecurity company has characterized FaceStealer as a victim acquisition platform that involves using compromised trusted contacts as a pathway to fuel a self-propagating attack chain via Telegram.

This includes hijacking social media and communications accounts such as Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord for extended periods of time, and then accessing the victim's contact list to target the victim's personal and professional circles.

The entire attack plays out as follows -

Compromise a victim: This involves harvesting cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, and other valuable access; hijacking their Telegram account or other communication app and locking them out; gaining access to their contacts and chat histories; and secretly recording them during the video chat.

Exploit the victim's Telegram account: The attacker impersonates the victim and sends tailored messages to other contacts on their behalf, proposing a Zoom or Teams meeting under the pretext of discussing an investment opportunity.

Set up the meeting: Should the target express interest, the attacker sends a Calendly invite via Telegram to schedule the video meeting. Shortly before the scheduled meeting time, the victim's Telegram account is used to send a typosquatted link that masquerades as a meeting URL for Zoom ("uu01webzoom[.]us") or Teams ("teams.livemeet[.]us").

Exploit recorded videos: When the target joins the fake Zoom meeting, the attacker plays an already recorded webcam video of the trusted contact and plays other videos, either recorded or deepfake videos, to give the impression that there are multiple participants in the meeting. In addition, headshot images generated using OpenAI ChatGPT are used as static avatar placeholders on the fake calls.

Trick the target into infecting themselves: The attacker sends a message to the target, claiming there is an audio issue or some other technical error (e.g., a deprecated Zoom SDK), and urges them to click on a link to apply an update to address the problem. Alternatively, it can take the form of running a script or copying and pasting malicious code into the command line or Terminal. This results in the deployment of malware that can capture sensitive data from the compromised device, effectively turning the target into the next victim.

Repeat the cycle: With the victim now compromised, the attacker gains control of their device and social media accounts to propagate the attack to their contacts.

Attacks mounted by BlueNoroff are known to specifically single out individuals working in the cryptocurrency and Web3 industries, along with individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.

The goal is to obtain access to the developers' devices and the software repository accounts they control to facilitate software supply chain attacks. Notably, the FaceStealer scheme was put to use in targeting the maintainer of the popular Axios npm package earlier this year to push a trojanized version that delivered a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT).

More than 900 victim webcam video recordings used by the threat actors to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks have been seized by the FBI. The agency said it's "aware of several other attempts by North Korean hackers to target software developers, maintainers, and software libraries with significant download volume."

In a report published in April 2026, Arctic Wolf said the targeted social engineering campaign had targeted over 400 victims across more than 20 countries, with most of them concentrated in the U.S., Singapore, the U.K., Hong Kong, South Korea, and the U.A.E.

Deepfake video production pipeline (credit: Arctic Wolf)

"A full 80% of identified targets operate directly in cryptocurrency/blockchain finance (54%) or adjacent finance and investment sectors (26%)," the cybersecurity company noted at the time. "CEOs and founders alone account for 45% of the target set – nearly half. This underscores BlueNoroff's singular operational focus: individuals with access to cryptocurrency assets, wallet infrastructure, exchange platforms, or investment decision-making authority."

The activity has since expanded in scope, with 677 targets identified across 58 countries. More than 80% of the targets are founders and C-suite executives. Besides introducing new lure themes such as a fake Chrome PDF Viewer update, the campaign incorporates generative AI technology from ChatGPT, Google, SpaceXAI Grok, and Wondershare AI Content Generator (AIGC) to supply the attackers with artwork, avatars, and convincing synthetic participant videos.

"Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate," the company added. "Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims' webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person's likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves."

BlueNoroff's updated attack flow (credit: Arctic Wolf)

Each new victim offers a pathway to further the attack. The cyclic modus operandi still remains the beating heart of the social engineering operation.

"Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff's efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships," Arctic Wolf said.

From FaceStealer to Contagious Interview

It's worth emphasizing here that the FaceStealer campaign is distinct from ClickFake Interview, an iteration of Contagious Interview that also employs ClickFix-style tactics to trigger the execution of malware as part of recruitment-themed campaigns.

Like FaceStealer, this involves the attackers approaching prospective targets by posing as recruiters on platforms like LinkedIn and sharing a "technical assessment" designed to run malware. In a post shared on LinkedIn, Alina Krasavina, an engineering manager at Delivery Hero, detailed how she was targeted in October 2026 by two fake recruiters on the same day, 13 minutes apart.

"The first one sent a 'technical assessment': a Next.js project of 113 files. At the end of next.config.js, after 204 spaces, there was a backdoor," Krasavina said. "The second one didn't send any ZIP. On a video call, a 'Member of Technical Staff' asked me to share my whole screen, download a repo, and run it. When I said no, he told me it was 'a requirement to continue.' After the call, I wrote to the recruiter and asked for another interview format. About a minute later she blocked me."

"The two attacks were built in opposite ways. The first one put the effort into the code and almost none into the recruiter. The second one put it into the people, and I never even saw its code."

According to a joint cybersecurity advisory published by cybersecurity and intelligence agencies from Japan, the U.S., Australia, and Germany in late September 2026, the long-running campaign is estimated to have compromised at least 30,000 devices located in 100 countries.

The attacks experiment with multiple delivery methods to convince victims to run malicious code -

Embedding malware in coding tests, repositories, or packages that victims are asked to run as part of an assessment process.

Using Microsoft Visual Studio Code (VS Code) tasks.json configuration files to automatically trigger the execution of malicious code when the project is opened in VS Code.

Using .githooks/pre-commit and post-checkout scripts to fire the malicious code on first commit or branch change.

Using trojanized installers for macOS utility apps to deliver OtterCookie by means of a shell script downloader.

Last month, Sophos disclosed that an employee's corporate macOS device had been compromised in mid-September 2026 after they cloned a public code repository presented as a job interview coding assignment and opened it as a workspace in VS Code.

"The repository contained a weaponized VS Code workspace settings file that replaced the editor's integrated terminal profile," the cybersecurity company said. "When a terminal opened in the workspace, the modified profile silently downloaded and ran a multi-stage payload."

The payload in question is BeaverTail, a JavaScript loader that's used to deliver a Python backdoor referred to as InvisibleFerret. Both malware families are attributed to Contagious Interview.

Sophos said the malware ran in memory on the device for about 26 hours, right from its execution on September 14, 2026, until it was rebooted a day later. The incident did not affect any of its products or services, or customer data or their systems, it added.

What's more, recent research from JFrog has uncovered that the threat actors linked to the campaign have even set up a decoy company named AccuraSoftHire, complete with a careers site, client testimonials, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards, and verified recruiters in an attempt to lend credibility and ultimately deceive candidates into running malware through a rigged take-home test and a video verification step.

"Our research shows these lures are built to pass the checks people rely on: a professional website, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards and recruiters with LinkedIn's verified badge," Guy Korolevski, senior security researcher at JFrog Security Research, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"Developers and other employees with system access can't be expected to catch that on their own, so employers need to set the rules. Interview assignments with downloads should only ever run in a disposable virtual machine, never on a work laptop. Security teams should also warn employees about downloading unknown files, even from a source they think they can trust. Developers can also check when a recruiter’s profile was created and whether the company's location is the same on every page."

Title: 354 dark web vendors and buyers arrested in Operation TorNado
Context: Europol’s 2026 Internet Organised Crime Threat Assessment names the replacement of shut-down markets as a current trend, with criminals moving fast to new platforms
Full Text:
Europol and police in 14 countries arrested 354 dark web vendors and buyers in Operation TorNado, which ran from May 2025 to October 2026. Investigators went after people who had traded on five marketplaces that were already offline: Archetyp, Bohemia, Nemesis, Kingdom and Tor2Door.

Seized money (Source: Europol)

The people who used those markets were still exposed after the sites went dark. Police also went after vendors and buyers on forums, single-vendor shops and encrypted messaging services, and carried out hundreds of house searches.

The US made the most arrests

The United States made 132 of the arrests. The UK followed with 59, then Hungary with 45 and Germany with 41. Finland made one arrest and conducted 159 interrogations.

US authorities seized more than 4.8 metric tonnes of drugs, 152 firearms and over €150 million in cash and cryptocurrency. In Europe, police seized 950 kilograms of drugs, 57 firearms, more than one million prescription tablets and over €60 million in cash and crypto. The US drug haul is about five times the size of Europe’s.

Europol traced the money

Europol sent staff to Czechia and Slovenia during the operation. It also coordinated the national cases so investigators didn’t end up chasing the same suspects twice. Its blockchain analysts traced the illegal transactions.

New markets keep appearing

TorNado follows earlier Europol operations, including RapTor in 2025, SpecTor in 2023, Dark Huntor in 2021 and DisrupTor in 2020. Europol’s 2026 Internet Organised Crime Threat Assessment names the replacement of shut-down markets as a current trend, with criminals moving fast to new platforms. The same assessment says marketplaces are splitting into platforms that each focus on one kind of crime.

Title: Operation Endgame Takes Down Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC Servers, Seizes 6.4M Stolen Logins
Context: Criminals used the three malware tools to gain access to computers, steal passwords, and launch ransomware attacks
Full Text:
An international police operation took down servers behind Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC this week. Criminals used the three malware tools to gain access to computers, steal passwords, and launch ransomware attacks.

Police also seized about 6.4 million stolen logins belonging to more than 40,000 victims, according to Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA).

Gootloader is a loader: once on a computer, it could download other malware, especially ransomware. It spread through fake legal documents placed on hacked websites, often WordPress sites. Criminals used SEO poisoning to push those sites high in search results.

Gootloader has infected at least 25,000 computers worldwide since 2018, the U.S. Justice Department said. Its operators used those computers to infect more computers, then sold access to the new ones to ransomware criminals. In the U.S., Gootloader was used in ransomware attacks against at least 44 victims, resulting in about $28.8 million in losses.

German police gave a much higher count in their statement in German. Based on what investigators know so far, Gootloader has infected millions of computers worldwide since it first appeared in 2020.

Across the three tools, police seized 235 servers and 257 domains, according to an operation summary from Europol, which supported the action. The takedown is part of Operation Endgame, an international police campaign against malware criminals use to access victims' computers.

For Gootloader, police took down 14 servers and 218 domains and removed malware from 681 hacked websites.

With court approval, U.S. agencies and their international partners removed Gootloader from more than 100 servers, including hacked WordPress sites. They also seized U.S. domains used to deliver and control the malware, according to the Justice Department announcement.

CastleRAT, a remote access trojan (RAT) known since 2025, allows attackers to control an infected computer remotely. Police seized 120 of its servers and 39 domains.

StealC is an infostealer that exfiltrates passwords and other login credentials from infected computers, allowing criminals to sell or misuse them. Police took down its servers again this week, after a June operation against it.

After that June action, its operators changed their infrastructure and brought it back online to stay out of investigators' reach, German police said. Some of StealC's key infrastructure ran on Virtualine/Omegatech, a bulletproof hosting service that advertised its services to criminals.

Police shut that hosting service down in a late-October takedown.

No arrests were announced in this week's action. Dutch police also carried out further investigations targeting Gootloader's main suspect, according to their news release.

What Victims and Site Owners Can Do

Dutch police have loaded data stolen by CastleRAT into Check your hack, a police service where people can enter an email address. If the address is in the data, the police send an email within a few minutes with steps to remove the malware. If it is not, no email arrives.

More data will be added in the coming weeks. The service checks single addresses, not whole domains, but organizations can join No More Leaks, a police project that shares data with private partners. The stolen data is also being shared with services including Have I Been Pwned and the Shadowserver Foundation.

Emails that claim to come from the police and ask people to check the data are fake. The police never send emails with links.

Even after police seize the data, criminals may still have the stolen logins, the police say in their frequently asked questions. As long as the malware stays on a computer, criminals may also keep getting its passwords.

The Shadowserver Foundation is working with internet service providers and computer security incident response teams (CSIRTs) to find infected computers and notify their owners, the Justice Department said. In Germany, the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) is helping notify victims, according to the BKA.

Denmark's National Special Crime Unit (NSK) helped clean the 681 websites. In a statement in Danish, the unit said it believes the attackers got into the sites with stolen passwords that came through criminal channels. They then installed a backdoor.

Officers removed the attackers' code and access, and left a message for the site owners with advice on securing their sites.

Police in Denmark and the Netherlands advise WordPress site owners to take these steps, several of which are set out in a Dutch advice sheet:

Change all administrator passwords to unique, at least 12-character passwords.

Turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA).

Remove accounts you do not recognize.

Remove any backdoor code from the site.

Update WordPress, its themes, and its plugins.

Allow access to the /wp-admin login page only from the IP addresses of your own devices.

Title: Law Enforcement Disrupts Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC Infrastructure
Context: Law enforcement agencies in the US, Europe, Australia, and Canada have seized infrastructure behind the notorious Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware
Full Text:
Law enforcement agencies in the US, Europe, Australia, and Canada have seized infrastructure behind the notorious Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware.

The investigators seized 235 servers and 257 domains associated with the malicious operations, severely crippling their distribution networks, Europol says.

Operating under the cybercrime-as-a-service model, Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC enabled ransomware attacks, data theft, and other cybercrime activities.

Distributed through compromised websites containing fake legal documents, Gootloader has been operating as a dropper for other malware families, including ransomware.

Active since at least 2018, Gootloader has infected over 25,000 computers and caused damages of approximately $28.8 million in the US, the US Department of Justice says.

According to the DoJ, the fresh disruption, part of Operation Endgame, led to the dropper’s removal from 100 servers. Europol reports that 14 servers and 218 domains associated with Gootloader were seized and 681 infected websites were cleaned up.

Title: Brit police watchdog says cops' use of facial recog risks wrongful arrests
Context: Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative...
Full Text: UK police forces must do more to prevent the wrongful arrests of people subjected to retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches, according to a Criminal Justice Inspectorate that holds deep concerns about the way in which the technology is used. According to a report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), there is a large gap in understanding among police forces and the National Crime Agency about how RFR should be used in responsible policing. The inspectorate blamed "fragmented and underdeveloped" frameworks for governance and legislation. It pointed to a lack of bespoke legislation to provide a uniform approach to police facial recognition use – and said existing laws have not kept pace with the technology. HMICFRS also said the rules governing each force's use of RFR are mismatched, and called for a statutory code to be included in the forthcoming Police Reform Bill to set nationwide standards. Illustrating the breadth of misunderstanding across forces, the report noted that despite the message being routinely communicated by National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) reps, individual investigators "often" thought RFR results constituted evidence rather than intelligence. In many cases, they are unaware that RFR results require further enquiries before enforcement action can be taken. "We found that some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches," the report stated. "In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action. "Although some forces had strengthened their processes after such incidents, practice remained inconsistent." Later in the report, the inspectorate described the findings as "deeply concerning." Some of the excuses police staff offered included acute demands on response teams leading to reduced opportunities to carry out further enquiries before acting on RFR matches. In one force, managers were known to encourage officers to "progress investigations quickly" after getting a match on the RFR system. However, the inspectorate clarified that just because an arrest is made, it does not necessarily mean it is wrongful, as investigators may need to rule out subjects from their inquiries. The onus for taking action should also be placed on the police forces themselves, given that some lack formal procedures regarding how RFR enquiries should be carried out, the report noted. The best forces had centralized facial recognition teams, which generally provided better governance and consistent processes. Officials fear long-term misuse of RFR, and other forms of facial recognition, will erode public trust in the technology, which it insists remains generally high. Surveys carried out in 2025 by the likes of the Ada Lovelace Institute and Alan Turing Institute, as well as the King's College London Policy Institute, showed a generally favorable view of facial recognition use in UK policing, with support ranging from 91 percent and 53 percent respectively. Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative experience. The Register's comments section often paints a vastly different picture of public perception of facial recognition. Kathryn Stone, his majesty's inspector at HMICFRS, said facial recognition has transformed policing, allowing officers to compare images in seconds, allowing them to solve crimes more quickly, but echoed the report's main concerns. "Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment," she said. "A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence." As well as legislative and governance-related concerns, HMICFRS also noted in its report that officers' training around the use of RFR remains inconsistent, and if improvements were made, this would lead to more effective and lawful use of RFR across the UK. Another major issue was police forces' failure to meet their image retention obligations. Forces were found too often to retain custody images taken of suspects on the Police National Database, against which many RFR queries are made. Police guidance sets out the scenarios in which custody images can and cannot be retained, and the inspectorate found that forces have failed to delete images that should have been wiped. The Police Reform Bill includes a provision to group custody images with the likes of DNA and fingerprints, bringing about more robust measures to ensure they are retained or deleted in line with legal requirements. A Home Office review previously found in 2017 that introducing such a statutory framework was untenable. It concluded that police could not automate the deletion of these images, and doing so manually would be too time-consuming. Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, said UK police cannot be allowed to continue to use RFR when it risks wrongfully arresting individuals. "The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming," she said. "This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they've never visited, as we've seen before. "Worse still, police aren't even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without any record of why they've been accused." Chaggar called on the government to "urgently step in" and help the UK's police forces to sort out the new frameworks needed for effective RFR use. ®

Full Text:
Authorities arrested 354 suspects in a joint international operation targeting vendors and buyers on the Archetyp, Nemesis, Tor2Door, Bohemia, and Kingdom dark web marketplaces.

Codenamed 'Operation TorNado,' this law enforcement action ran from May 2025 to October 2026 and involved agencies from 14 countries.

"Additionally, law enforcement targeted vendors and buyers active on forums, single-vendor shops, and encrypted messaging services. National authorities conducted independent investigations with Europol's support, including cross-checks via SIENA and forensic analysis," Europol said.

"The operation highlighted the evolving resilience of dark web marketplaces, which continue to adapt despite takedowns."

They seized over €60 million ($66 million) in cash and cryptocurrency, 950 kilograms of illicit drugs (including amphetamines, cocaine, ketamine, psilocybin mushrooms, MDMA, and cannabis), and 57 firearms in Europe.

"Following the takedown of multiple darknet marketplaces and vendor targets in the previous JCODE operation, U.S. and international law enforcement agencies obtained intelligence to identify Dark Web drug traffickers, resulting in a series of complementary, but separate, law enforcement investigations," the US Department of Justice added.

"By leveraging complementary partnerships and surging resources across the U.S. government and Europol, Operation TorNado significantly disrupted the online opioid trade and sends a strong message that criminals operating on the Dark Web are not beyond the reach of law enforcement."

Operation TorNado follows several similar actions over the last six years, including DisrupTor in 2020 (which led to 179 arrests) and Dark Huntor in 2021 (in which 150 more high-volume darknet vendors were apprehended).

In April 2022, US authorities and German police also took down Hydra, the world's largest dark web marketplace at the time, with more than 19,000 seller accounts that were serving over 17 million customers worldwide.

One year later, in 2023, Operation SpecTor led to the arrest of 288 other suspects who allegedly sold illicit drugs on dark web markets and the seizure of €50.8 million ($55.9 million) in cash and cryptocurrency.

More recently, in May 2025, law enforcement also announced the arrest of another 270 dark web vendors and buyers from ten countries as part of Operation RapTor.

Title: Police dismantle Gootloader, CastleRAT, StealC malware infrastructure
Context: "Victim data will be made available via platforms HaveIBeenPwned, DIVD, CheckjeHack, NoMoreLeaks, Sekoia, The Shadowserver Foundation, and NL-NCSC, alerting victims of stolen...
Full Text:
Europol and law enforcement partners from nine countries have seized hundreds of servers and domains used by the Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware operations.

Gootloader is a malware loader active since 2020, StealC is an infostealer that helps exfiltrate credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and other sensitive information from victims' devices, and CastleRAT is a remote access trojan that surfaced last year. All three malware families have been used by various cybercriminal operations, including ransomware gangs.

The joint action is part of Operation Endgame, an international law enforcement effort targeting cybercrime and "cybercrime-as-a-service" networks. This stage of Operation Endgame included law enforcement agencies from Bulgaria, Canada, Denmark, Germany, Moldova, the Netherlands, Poland, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with Europol and Eurojust coordinating the effort.

Together with private partners who helped identify, take down, seize, and block infrastructure tied to the three malware operations, the authorities seized 257 domains and 235 servers.

They also identified 6.4 million victim datasets on the targeted criminal infrastructure, stolen from malware-infected systems for use in other cyberattacks, including ransomware breaches.

"During the action, over 6 million victim credentials were identified in the criminal infrastructure owned by the cybercriminals and seized by the authorities during this week. The suspects were using these credentials, stolen from the victims after they infected them, to sell them and later be used for other cyber-attacks such as ransomware," Europol said.

"Victim data will be made available via platforms HaveIBeenPwned, DIVD, CheckjeHack, NoMoreLeaks, Sekoia, The Shadowserver Foundation, and NL-NCSC, alerting victims of stolen credentials caused by the CastleRAT malware. WordPress users are urged to update credentials, enable multi-factor authentication, and patch vulnerabilities."

Previous Operation Endgame actions

In June, as part of the same operation, law enforcement agencies also cleaned nearly 15,000 malware-infected WordPress websites and seized 106 servers used by the SocGholish botnet and the Evil Corp Russian cybercrime group.

Later that month, Operation Endgame disrupted malicious infrastructure used by the Amadey and StealC malware operations, taking down 326 servers and 142 domains and recovering around 27 million credentials stolen from more than 385,000 compromised systems.

One year ago, the same joint law enforcement action also took down over 1,000 servers used by the Rhadamanthys, VenomRAT, and Elysium botnet malware operations.

Previously, Operation Endgame targeted Smokeloader botnet customers and servers, ransomware infrastructure, the AVCheck site, and various other major malware operations, including DanaBot, IcedID, Pikabot, Trickbot, Smokeloader, Bumblebee, and SystemBC.

Title: Check Point Expands Its FedRAMP Certification to Include Check Point WAF

Full Text:
The federal, state, local government, and education sectors are under growing cyber pressure, and the attack surface is shifting to where they now serve citizens most. According to Check Point’s 2026 Cyber Security Report, government organizations faced an average of 2,680 cyber-attacks per organization each week in 2025, a 17% increase from 2024, making government the second most targeted sector worldwide. As government organizations move services online, deploy citizen self-service portals, connect APIs, and integrate AI into mission-critical workflows, every new capability creates a new entry point. A successful attack doesn’t just disrupt IT-it can interrupt essential services, expose sensitive citizen records, compromise internal secrets, and undermine public trust.

The data reflects that reality. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report recorded 3,634 public-sector incidents and 2,410 confirmed data disclosure breaches, with exploitation of vulnerabilities accounting for 40% of initial access, and personal data, internal data, and secrets among the most compromised. That makes runtime web application and API protection especially critical for government organizations running legacy systems, third-party applications, and public-facing services that cannot always be patched immediately.

Check Point has been addressing this risk inside government trust and compliance requirements since achieving FedRAMP Certification for its Check Point Platform for Government in 2025. Now Check Point is expanding its FedRAMP-Certified packages to include Check Point WAF, bringing prevention-first web application security, API protection, Bot mitigation, DDoS defence, CDN-integrated delivery, and GenAI application security into the same government-certified platform.

Security Built for Modern Government Applications

Government organizations no longer operate static websites. Today’s public sector runs digital citizen portals, API-driven benefit and payment systems, cloud-native applications, and AI-enabled interfaces that connect identity, records, contractors, and partner organizations across the public sector. This growing interconnection makes the application layer more dynamic, complex, and exposed.

AI is also transforming both the speed of attacks and the security model required to stop them. Frontier AI technologies demonstrate how vulnerabilities can be discovered and validated autonomously at unprecedented speed and scale. Attackers are already using AI-powered tools to generate payload variations and exploit weaknesses faster, making signature-based protection increasingly ineffective. As a result, pre-emptive, AI-driven prevention that can stop unknown attacks without signatures or emergency updates is becoming essential.

Modern Web Application and API Protection (WAAP) must secure far more than a single website or API endpoint. Government organizations need prevention-first protection across the entire application environment, including:

Pre-emptively prevent known, unknown, and zero-day web and API attacks before they reach the application

End-to-end API security with automated discovery, schema validation and authentication enforcement

Availability of critical services with strong bot mitigation and DDoS protection against automated abuse and disruption

Block GenAI application attacks including prompt injection, data leakage and harmful content

Simplify operations with centralized management that reduces tool sprawl and complexity across the full application stack

Check Point WAF brings all these capabilities into a single consolidated platform, purpose-built for the modern application reality that government organizations face today. By adding it to the FedRAMP certified packages, federal organizations can now secure public-facing applications and APIs through the same government-certified platform they already trust with the prevention, visibility, and control needed to protect modern application environments without adding complexity or managing separate tools for every risk.

Why This Matters Now

The public-sector application attack surface is expanding quickly as government organizations modernize services, expose more APIs, and begin adopting AI-enabled workflows. At the same time, AI is accelerating the speed at which attackers find and exploit those weaknesses.

According to Check Point 2026 Cloud Security Report, 70% of organizations run GenAI workloads in production, yet visibility has not kept up. Only 5% of organizations have full visibility into how AI is used, and just 14% actively enforce and audit an AI security policy.

PHP2Shell shows how fast the window closes. Two critical PHP flaws, each rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale, let an attacker run code on a server with one crafted request, with no password, account, or user interaction. Attacks started before the patch landed on October 21, 2026, and government organizations took sites offline to cope. Check Point WAF preemptively blocked PHP2Shell with no signature, rule, or configuration change.

This is why expanding Check Point’s FedRAMP certification packages to include Check Point WAF matters. It is not just another security product. It is a way to help public-sector organizations protect the applications, APIs, and digital services that citizens, employees, contractors, and partners depend on every day.

Available Through the FedRAMP Marketplace

Check Point is listed on the FedRAMP Marketplace, with Check Point WAF included in the certification, making it easier for federal mission owners to discover, evaluate, and procure the solution.

Title: NCSC Launches Cyber Adversary Testing to Boost Resilience
Context: The UK’s leading cybersecurity agency has officially launched a new scheme designed to help providers of critical infrastructure to test and improve their cyber resilience
Full Text:
The UK’s leading cybersecurity agency has officially launched a new scheme designed to help providers of critical infrastructure to test and improve their cyber resilience.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) first trailed its Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme at the CYBERUK 2025 conference.

It enables participating organizations to choose from a list of vetted suppliers, who then craft realistic attack plans based on reconnaissance of the client’s IT infrastructure, exposure, and threat landscape.

“Testers adopt an adversarial mindset and use appropriate tools and techniques to achieve agreed objectives, rather than being driven by commercially procured threat intelligence or constrained by documented tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs),” the NCSC said.

Read more on cyber resilience: NCSC: Observability and Threat Hunting Must Improve

The CyAS scheme is designed to complement other NCSC initiatives including the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and the associated Cyber Resilience Audit (CRA).

It’s hoped that larger organizations, CNI providers, and government bodies in particular use these frameworks to better understand their security posture and resilience.

“By enabling rigorous, realistic end-to-end assessments by the very best adversary simulation experts, CyAS will help organizations build a clearer picture of how they would stand up to genuine cyber-attacks and take action to strengthen their security and resilience,” said NCSC CTO, Ollie Whitehouse.

“Ultimately, stronger resilience across the UK helps prepare the country for crisis by protecting the essential services we all rely on every day from the most pressing threats.”

Building Resilience for the Future

Andrew Costis, engineering manager of the Adversary Research Team at AttackIQ, welcomed the program's potential to help organizations test how well they can keep essential services running during an attack.

“Building each simulation around an organization’s actual exposure should uncover weaknesses that a generic assessment might miss. Looking back, that approach could have exposed gaps in detection or containment before an intrusion became a prolonged outage,” he said.

“The longer-term opportunity is turning those findings into an ongoing practice through adversarial exposure validation.”

Costis explained that teams must repeat attack behaviors after remediating a weakness to check that the fix has worked, and adapt their testing over time as environments change.

“An assured provider gives organisations confidence in the assessment’s quality,” he concluded. “Keeping those lessons current will determine how much resilience the scheme delivers.”

CyAS will initially operate as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), so that the NCSC can test demand, refine its methodology, and build confidence before moving towards a fuller operating model.

In this article

A former FBI supervisor stole from cryptocurrency wallets involved in 35 FBI investigations

He planned to use the proceeds to finance a new life in Portugal

He turned himself in after confessing to a former colleague

Law enforcement officers are trusted to handle sensitive evidence properly. A 37-year-old former FBI supervisor used that access to steal millions in cryptocurrency.

Patrick Steven Yaroch pleaded guilty on November 5 to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million from cryptocurrency wallets linked to FBI investigations.

He stole the money from wallets held by people the FBI was investigating, which included adversarial nation-state actors. Starting no later than December 2024, he made around 100 transfers using credentials tied to 35 separate investigations.

The FBI’s search affidavit says that Yaroch accessed FBI systems containing wallet seed phrases and memorized them. A seed phrase is a series of words, commonly 12 or 24, used to restore access to a cryptocurrency wallet. Anyone with the seed phrase can potentially control the funds.

He then used the memorized phrases to transfer funds to a personal wallet on his own device. He subsequently swapped assets into different currencies and made further transactions to try and hide their origins.

According to the Department of Justice (DOJ), his actions compromised multiple investigations.

The affidavit also revealed that Yaroch had asked ChatGPT how to invest a million dollars, along with advice on where to live in Europe. It suggested Portugal, and he began the process of setting up a life there.

Caught by a case of cold feet

According to the affidavit, he approached a former DOJ colleague to confess because his actions were “eating him up inside.” The employee urged him to self-report, which he did.

The FBI placed him on leave and then terminated his employment two days later. They showed up at his home with a warrant and seized assets, including his phone, which had access to a Kraken cryptocurrency account. They also seized a piece of paper containing the seed phrases for his own account.

More law enforcement corruption

Yaroch’s justification for his initial actions was frustration that the FBI wasn’t acting quickly enough against the wallets’ criminal owners. So he decided to “take matters into his own hands,” according to the affidavit.

But according to the DOJ, he also used some of the proceeds to cover personal debts, including credit cards, car payments, and other loans.

This isn’t an isolated incident. In December 2024, former Secret Service agent Anthony Joseph Evans pleaded guilty to stealing cryptocurrency worth $56,000 from a hardware wallet held in the agency’s secure evidence vault.

In 2015, former Secret Service agent Shaun W. Bridges also pleaded guilty to money laundering and obstruction of justice after stealing bitcoin during the investigation of Silk Road, a dark web marketplace used to sell illegal drugs and other contraband. He used another person’s administrator account to reset users’ passwords and move bitcoin into a wallet he controlled. The stolen bitcoin was worth approximately $350,000 at the time; he later sold it for $820,000.

Title: NCSC scheme will help critical organisations test their cyber defences
Context: A key feature of the CyAS methodology is that providers conduct reconnaissance to understand the customer’s technology, exposure and threat landscape
Full Text:
The NCSC has launched a new Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme.

The scheme is designed to help strengthen national cyber resilience, supporting the UK's most critical organisations, as well as overseeing bodies.

The scheme assures suppliers of cyber adversary simulation services, helping organisations identify trusted providers to test their defences and their ability to prevent, detect and respond to realistic simulated cyber attacks.

Like all NCSC Industry Assurance schemes, CyAS draws on the NCSC’s expertise as the UK’s National Technical Authority for cyber security. Commercial providers are assessed against an NCSC-defined standard, giving organisations confidence that they are buying services that meet recognised requirements.

A key feature of the CyAS methodology is that providers conduct reconnaissance to understand the customer’s technology, exposure and threat landscape. This is then used to develop realistic, customer-specific attack plans. Testers adopt an adversarial mindset and use appropriate tools and techniques to achieve agreed objectives, rather than being driven by commercially procured threat intelligence or constrained by documented tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs).

The scheme complements other NCSC frameworks that support cyber regulation, including the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and the associated Cyber Resilience Audit (CRA) scheme. Together, these frameworks will help organisations - particularly larger organisations, those operating in critical national infrastructure and government - build a clearer picture of their cyber security and resilience.

They also give Cyber Oversight Bodies a trusted way to gather evidence of resilience across the sectors they oversee. This supports consistency, shared learning and a stronger understanding of cyber risk.

Speaking at the launch, the NCSC’s Chief Technology Officer Ollie Whitehouse said:

You cannot improve what you do not know. That is why I am delighted to see the launch of the Cyber Adversary Simulation scheme. By enabling rigorous, realistic end to end assessments by the very best adversary simulation experts, CyAS will help organisations build a clearer picture of how they would stand up to genuine cyber attacks and take action to strengthen their security and resilience.

“Ultimately, stronger resilience across the UK helps prepare the country for crisis by protecting the essential services we all rely on every day from the most pressing threats.

NCSC Deputy Director Chris Ensor added:

Moving beyond traditional pen testing and auditing of controls, the CyAS service enables organisations to practically test their cyber defences, ensuring they are able to protect, detect and respond to cyber attacks.

CyAS has been developed in partnership with Cyber Oversight Bodies, including regulators and Lead Government Departments, to establish a common core standard and a more consistent approach to demonstrating cyber resilience.

The scheme will initially operate as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), enabling the NCSC to test demand, refine the methodology and build confidence before moving towards a fuller operating model.

You can find a full list of assured service providers on the schemes ‘Find a Provider’ page.

Title: Railway Says Stolen Customer AI Keys Led to $740,000 in Estimated Unauthorized Usage Charges
Context: At 07:28 UTC on October 20, the attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partly escape the filesystem isolation around a build and read some files on the host virtual...
Full Text:
AI provider keys that customers stored on Railway were stolen in an October breach and used to commit an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized spending, the platform-as-a-service provider said yesterday. It has promised to pay those charges itself when an AI provider will not refund them.

The company builds and runs apps for its customers and stores their secrets, such as API keys and database credentials, as environment variables. The attacker decrypted variables in at most 1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, and its database queries looked for AI provider keys.

In an October 26 update, the company told customers asking about refunds for unauthorized AI spend that "Railway is unable to refund customers for spend performed with compromised API keys." It encouraged them to contact the AI providers directly and offered to escalate their requests.

According to the company's incident report, the decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users: BYOK agent keys and GitHub OAuth tokens. All were reset, each user was notified, and no logins to customer accounts using stolen credentials were found.

In addition to AI keys, one of the attacker's database queries matched cloud, database, and payment service credentials. The company's forensics did not show any customer databases being accessed, and there was no indication that customers' code repositories were downloaded.

The attacker also read the stored histories of 353 builds, including the variables and secrets passed to those builds.

The company's logs show which environments were exposed but not which variables, so the figure of about 100,000 workspaces is an upper limit. It emailed customers it judged to be at high risk.

Any data the attacker copied but did not decrypt can no longer be decrypted, because the credential the attacker used has been disabled, according to the company.

What Railway Customers Can Do

Refund terms differ by AI provider, according to the company's incident report:

AWS Bedrock: AWS's existing refund policy covers fraud, and its account teams have started refunds.

Google Gemini: Google's existing refund policy covers fraud, and its account teams have started refunds.

OpenAI: Refunds are reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Customers file a claim with OpenAI, then pass the case ID to Railway's support team.

SpaceXSI: Refunds are reviewed on a case-by-case basis, and customers submit their claims to the same support team.

Anthropic: Talks are still underway, and the platform will cover costs from breached Anthropic keys in the meantime.

OpenRouter: It maintains its no-refund policy in its terms of service, so the platform will cover all OpenRouter-related costs resulting from the breach.

Customers are asked to report charges they did not make through a charge report form. The form says the company "is not responsible for usage of these keys" but is investigating the theft and working with the providers.

The report does not say how the $740,000 figure was estimated or what period it covers. Neither it nor the form sets a cap or a deadline for claims, or states whether customers must pay disputed charges while a claim is under review.

The company advises customers to revoke and replace any sensitive variable stored on the platform before October 21. Keys should be revoked or rotated with the provider that issued them, since filing a charge report does not revoke a key.

It also advises removing public network access to databases, checking GitHub audit logs and which apps can access the account, and checking audit logs in registries such as Docker Hub. Most of this advice dates from the company's October disclosure and a report it published the next day.

Out of caution, the company also gave some providers every key it held for their services, so reset requests reached more than 100,000 users. A revocation notice from a provider does not by itself mean a key was exposed.

How the Railway Breach Happened

The attack began in the company's build system, according to its incident report. At 07:28 UTC on October 20, the attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partly escape the filesystem isolation around a build and read some files on the host virtual machine.

That gave the attacker a credential that build servers use to push finished images and reach some internal systems. The on-call engineer was paged at 13:58 UTC, about six and a half hours after the first exploit, when an alert flagged unusual calls to a registry service.

The credential was meant only for build work, but the company's internal Temporal system, which drives parts of the build process, accepted it as a trusted client. Through it, the attacker read some stored histories of other builds.

The same credential could also fetch cached snapshots of code. That gave the attacker a copy of the company's internal monorepo, the code base that many of its services deploy from. The company says the copy showed the attacker how the platform works and helped them find exploits and move quickly between systems.

After scanning that code, the attacker found a wrongly configured OIDC binding in one of the company's cloud environments. The binding is part of how its deployment system obtains short-lived cloud credentials, and at 03:26 UTC on October 21, the attacker exploited the mistake to obtain one.

With that credential, the attacker took two more from the cloud environment. One could read encrypted variables from a production database when used inside the internal network, and the other was an SSH key.

The SSH key opened a machine that runs orchestration tasks for the company's fleet. That machine stored a credential capable of decrypting customer variables, which it needed to start customer workloads.

Each environment's variables are encrypted with that environment's own key, and those keys are, in turn, encrypted by a root key stored in a cloud provider's key management service (KMS).

Between 04:07 and 05:21 UTC on October 21, the attacker pulled encrypted variables from the database, looking for names that matched AI provider keys. Using the orchestration machine's credentials with the KMS, it decrypted some of them between 04:42 and 05:14 UTC and again between 06:36 and 07:15 UTC.

The attacker was fully removed from the company's systems at 09:24 UTC that day.

Those times differ from the company's preliminary report of October 22, which dated the attack from 13:58 UTC on October 20 and placed decryption after 05:27 UTC.

Each build now runs in its own short-lived virtual machine, on top of the old isolation. Its credentials can push only one specific image to the company's registry.

Within an hour of the company patching the original escape, its own hardening team built a second exploit by changing that attack. That was one reason the company moved every user to the new build system at once.

Every weakness the attacker used is now closed, the company says. It has filed a complaint with the FBI's IC3 and is working with a specialist forensics firm whose investigation continues.

It is sharing indicators of compromise privately for now and plans to publish them once law enforcement agrees.

The company believes the stolen credentials were used by services that relay or resell access to AI providers for use in distillation. It has not established whether the attacker ran those services, nor has it named the attacker.

In their Black October analysis, Wiz researchers list this breach among incidents disclosed in October by at least nine AI developer platforms, including the earlier OpenCode breach.

Every public report describes attackers hunting for stored environment variables, especially ones that grant AI access, the researchers say. No single flaw or software dependency links the attacks.
