Title: The next name on CISA's door.
Context: The streamlined questionnaire collects more granular incident data—categorizing intrusions across malware, social engineering, and insider threats—while integrating the MITRE ATT&CK framework to align observations with known adversary techniques. While only civilian federal agencies face mandatory reporting...
Full Text:
Palantir’s CISO gets the nod for CISA. Tehran takes the rap for sabotaging European grocery freezers. Russia’s Turla turns victim Exchange servers into passive spy hubs. Barracuda battles actively chained gateway zero-days. Vanderbilt grapples with a BYOD ransomware outbreak. CISA rushes patches for critical IBM and SignalWire flaws, while revamping its national incident portal. ENISA tracks the EU’s cyber maturity gap. Cryptographers debate whether AI will crack modern encryption. Our guest is Duncan Greatwood, CEO at Xage Security, discussing the cybersecurity problem you can’t patch away. Chinese AI labs set up shop in Silicon Valley's backyard.

Today is Tuesday November 10th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Trump nominates Palantir’s CISO to lead CISA.

The White House has tapped private-sector defense experience to take the helm at CISA.

President Trump nominated Michael LoSapio, chief information security officer at Palantir Technologies, to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The nomination was sent to the Senate on November ninth and awaits confirmation. If approved, LoSapio will succeed acting director Nick Andersen as the agency’s Senate-confirmed leader.

LoSapio brings over twenty years of systems engineering, cloud infrastructure, and cybersecurity experience to the role. At Palantir, he directed defenses against sophisticated nation-state adversaries, following earlier infrastructure roles at SingleStore and high-performance computing engineering at New York University.

The nomination was announced in an official statement from the White House.

CISA upgrades incident reporting portal with MITRE ATT&CK taxonomy.

CISA is revamping how organizations report cyber incidents, leaning on standardized frameworks to turn disparate breach alerts into actionable national intelligence.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency rolled out an updated reporting form on its Incident Reporting Portal. The streamlined questionnaire collects more granular incident data—categorizing intrusions across malware, social engineering, and insider threats—while integrating the MITRE ATT&CK framework to align observations with known adversary techniques. While only civilian federal agencies face mandatory reporting requirements under FISMA, CISA urges all critical infrastructure operators to voluntarily submit disclosures.

Standardizing intake across public and private sectors enables analysts to spot broader adversary campaigns faster, proving that one enterprise's early detection can secure an entire ecosystem.

Details were announced in an official agency release citing CISA’s Chris Butera.

ENISA charts EU cyber maturity amid AI and infrastructure threats.

The European Union is taking stock of its collective cyber defenses, and while overall maturity is climbing, the regional threat ecosystem refuses to stand still.

According to ENISA’s biennial State of Cybersecurity in the Union report, the bloc averaged 71.5 points out of 100 on its 2026 Cybersecurity Index. Executive Director Juhan Lepassaar credited robust supply chain governance and research initiatives, but cautioned that recent disruptions—including cyber incidents hitting industrial refrigeration systems—spotlight persistent operational gaps. The assessment also identified uneven incident response capabilities among national CSIRTs alongside an expanding global cyber skills shortage.

While legislative frameworks like the NIS2 Directive push baseline compliance, operational realities diverge as frontier artificial intelligence accelerates automated vulnerability discovery and ideologically driven hacktivism dominates incident volume.

ENISA published the report in cooperation with the European Commission and the NIS Cooperation Group under Article 18 of the NIS2 Directive.

Western officials link Iranian cyber unit to European supermarket sabotage.

State-sponsored cyber sabotage has crossed into everyday retail operations across Europe, spoiling tens of millions of dollars in food.

French officials, backed by American investigators, have tied a wave of cyber incidents affecting supermarket freezers and refrigerators across at least six European nations to Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In France alone, actors remotely altered temperatures at over seven hundred supermarkets, forcing units into defrost cycles and triggering fires and equipment failures. The Paris prosecutor is now pursuing international arrest warrants for the group's leadership.

Targeting internet-accessible industrial control systems reveals a deliberate pivot toward low-complexity, high-impact civilian disruption, testing Western infrastructure resilience well beyond conventional military targets.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced the attribution during a G-7 gathering in Paris, while U.S. and European agencies continue ongoing investigations.

Cryptographers debate whether AI advances could unravel modern encryption.

While cybersecurity planners have spent years preparing for quantum decryption, a nearer-term challenge may be arriving from artificial intelligence.

Advances in machine learning are accelerating mathematical discoveries, prompting some researchers to question whether algorithmic shortcuts might unravel the foundational math securing modern encryption. Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green points to recent breakthroughs in theoretical computer science, while Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin has called for the industry to proactively develop “post-AI cryptography.”

However, other leading voices urge restraint. Coinbase head of cryptography Yehuda Lindell contends that current post-quantum algorithms are resilient, arguing that speculative panic is premature and that artificial intelligence is just as likely to help defend and harden existing cryptographic primitives.

At stake is the core premise of modern digital trust: if computational shortcuts render previously intractable mathematical problems solvable, upgrading legacy protocols before adversaries exploit them becomes a race against time.

Attackers chain Barracuda ESG flaws for root access in targeted attacks.

Barracuda Networks is urging administrators to patch immediately as threat actors actively target two critical vulnerabilities in its Email Security Gateway appliances.

Tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, the flaws allow attackers with access to an appliance's administrative interface to bypass authorization controls and execute arbitrary commands with root privileges. While patched last week, Barracuda confirmed on Monday that attackers are already exploiting the chained flaws against a limited number of customer environments. Several other Barracuda products, including its Load Balancer and Web Application Firewall, share the command injection vulnerability.

Securing perimeter email gateways remains a priority for enterprise defense, especially given past nation-state campaigns that weaponized edge appliances for persistent espionage.

Turla deploys stealthy "Cereal" malware targeting Exchange servers.

Russian state-sponsored operators are turning victim email servers into their own operational infrastructure.

ESET Research has detailed "Cereal," a sophisticated, modular .NET malware toolkit attributed to the Russian threat group Turla. Deployed against national government bodies in Kazakhstan and Romania, the malware eliminates dedicated external command-and-control servers. Instead, a passive backdoor listens for incoming malicious web requests disguised as legitimate Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync traffic. Another module, CerealBox, injects directly into Exchange's transport service, in-memory hijacking existing mail handlers to filter and stage messages involving NATO and European Union addresses.

By operating entirely within legitimate enterprise processes and unmanaged .NET image caches, the campaign evades traditional network defenses while weaponizing mission-critical servers as long-term intelligence collection hubs.

Vanderbilt University investigates a cyberattack claimed by BYOD ransomware.

Vanderbilt University is actively responding to a significant cybersecurity incident affecting campus devices, enterprise systems, and cloud infrastructure.

University officials instructed students, faculty, and staff on Monday to power down institutional hardware, disconnect from campus Wi-Fi, and alert IT to suspicious behavior. While the university has not officially confirmed the specific nature of the intrusion, the relatively new BYOD ransomware gang claimed responsibility on its data leak site. The group claims to have encrypted databases and exfiltrated research files alongside personal records for over one million individuals.

Targeting major academic research hubs underscores how rapidly evolving ransomware operations threaten both critical intellectual property and sensitive community data.

CISA adds actively exploited IBM and SignalWire bugs to KEV catalog.

CISA has added critical vulnerabilities affecting IBM Aspera Faspex and SignalWire FreeSwitch to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Both flaws carry CVSS scores of 9.8. The Faspex bug permits authorization bypass for full administrative takeover, while the FreeSwitch defect enables arbitrary command execution via crafted SIP messages. Mandated under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal civilian agencies must apply vendor patches within three days.

Rapid cataloging of these flaws underscores federal urgency to seal network-accessible enterprise tools before widespread automated exploitation takes hold.

On our Industry Voices segment, I sat down with Duncan Greatwood, CEO at Xage Security, discussing the cybersecurity problem you can’t patch away. Here’s our conversation.

If you enjoyed this conversation be sure to check out the show notes for the full interview.

Chinese AI labs set up shop in Silicon Valley's backyard.

Chinese AI companies are taking their talent search straight to Silicon Valley, hoping to recruit the researchers who helped make American AI labs dominant.

MiniMax, Moonshot, and ByteDance are expanding their U.S. hiring efforts, targeting engineers with experience at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.

But there's a problem. American AI researchers are expensive, with top talent commanding compensation packages exceeding a million dollars annually. Chinese companies generally have smaller budgets, and researchers often prefer working on cutting-edge American models.

There's also the matter of work-life balance. China's notorious “996” schedule—nine to nine, six days a week—is apparently not a particularly compelling recruiting perk.

ByteDance is reportedly offering substantially higher compensation to compete, but money isn't everything.

Meanwhile, Washington's restrictions on Chinese access to advanced technology could eventually extend to talent recruitment.

For now, Chinese AI companies can open offices in Silicon Valley. Convincing Silicon Valley's engineers to join them is another matter.

CMMC: Understanding the Difference Between a POA&M and an OPA

November 10, 2026

Jason Spencer

BLOG

5 min.

Understanding the difference between a Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M) and an Operational Plan of Action (OPA) starts with recognizing that these two documents serve different purposes under 32 CFR Part 170 (the CMMC Program).

TL;DR – LA Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M) and an Operational Plan of Action (OPA) serve fundamentally different purposes under CMMC and confusing the two is one of the fastest ways to stall your certification.

A POA&M is tied to a C3PAO assessment finding, carries a 180-day closure deadline and directly impacts certification

An OPA tracks temporary vulnerabilities found during normal operations with no fixed timeline or certification consequence

Most compliance failures come from documentation mistakes, not security gaps

The Key Attributes of a POA&M and OPA

A POA&M is a formal remediation plan created in response to a C3PAO assessment finding where a security requirement is marked “Not Met”. It carries a strict 180-day closure deadline and directly impacts CMMC certification. An OPA, by contrast, tracks temporary vulnerabilities discovered during normal operations and carries no fixed deadline or certification consequence.

The following table provides a side-by-side comparison of the key attributes that distinguish these two documents.

Attribute

POA&M (Plan of Action & Milestones)

OPA (Operational Plan of Action)

Purpose

Documents NOT MET security requirements found during a CMMC assessment; tracks remediation to full compliance

Documents ongoing operational security activities, continuous improvement and risk management

Time-Bound

Yes — strict 180-day remediation deadline

No — ongoing with no fixed deadline

Trigger

Created when a practice is scored NOT MET during a C3PAO assessment

Created proactively as part of ongoing security operations

Certification Impact

Allows conditional CMMC Level 2 certification

Cannot cover or paper over a NOT MET requirement

Eligible Practices

Only 1-point practices (up to 22 maximum)

Applies broadly to operational improvements and enhancements

Score Threshold

Must score 80% or higher (88/110 practices MET)

No scoring threshold — exists independently of assessment

Close-Out

Formal close-out assessment by C3PAO within 180 days

Reviewed and updated as part of continuous monitoring; no formal close-out

Failure Consequence

Loses conditional certification if not remediated within 180 days

No direct certification consequence; may become findings in future assessments

Nature

Reactive — addresses deficiencies found during assessment

Proactive — addresses planned improvements and ongoing risk management

What Must a POA&M and an OPA Include to Pass a CMMC Assessment?

Knowing the difference between a POA&M and an OPA is only the first step. Organizations must also understand what each document needs to contain to satisfy assessor expectations and regulatory requirements. A strong POA&M goes beyond acknowledging a gap. It must include defined remediation steps, responsible parties, resource and budget requirements, milestones with specific dates and a firm 180-day closure commitment. A strong OPA must clearly identify the temporary vulnerability, describe the mitigation or correction plan, outline the current risk posture and explain the monitoring approach.

The table below breaks down the required content elements for each document type.

Strong POA&M Must Include

Strong OPA Must Include

Clear explanation of what is missing and why

Defined remediation steps with responsible parties

Resource requirements and budget implications

Milestones with specific completion dates

Evidence of active progress toward closure

180-day closure deadline commitment

Identification of the temporary vulnerability or deficiency

Explanation of how it will be mitigated, corrected or eliminated

Current risk posture description

Monitoring and tracking approach

No fixed deadline required - duration depends on circumstances

8 of the Most Common POA&M and OPA Mistakes Under CMMC

Even organizations with mature security programs frequently stumble when preparing POA&Ms and OPAs for CMMC compliance. These mistakes range from treating routine vulnerabilities as OPA items (when standard vulnerability management processes under RA.L2-3.11.3 and SI.L1-3.14.1 should apply) to submitting vague timelines that assessors will immediately flag. Other common errors include omitting required mitigation details from OPAs, resubmitting pre-CMMC implementation plans as POA&Ms, assuming compliance without completing a gap assessment or collecting actual evidence, making CUI scoping errors, practices not eligible for the POA&M and preparing for the wrong assessment criteria entirely.

The table below outlines eight of the most frequent mistakes and explains why each one matters.

#

Mistake

Why It Matters

1

Treating routine vulnerabilities as OPA items

Not every vulnerability warrants an OPA. Use standard vulnerability management (RA.L2-3.11.3 / SI.L1-3.14.1) instead.

2

Using vague timelines in POA&Ms

Assessors expect specific dates, resources and checkpoints - not general language.

3

Leaving mitigation details out of the OPA

CA.L2-3.12.2 requires documenting how deficiencies will be mitigated, corrected or eliminated.

4

Resubmitting the NIST SP 800-171 implementation POA&M

A pre-CMMC project plan is not a POA&M for assessment findings; these are distinct documents.

5

Assumed compliance without evidence

Organizations often assume compliance without completing a gap assessment or actual evidence collection.

6

CUI scoping errors

Organizations fail to understand FCI and/or CUI contracts and flows in their environment.

7

Preparing for the wrong assessment criteria

Failing to identify FCI for Level 1 or CUI for Level 2 compliance.

8

Practices not eligible for POA&M inclusion

Not POA&M eligible practices and objectives will lead to failure self-assessment and C3PAO assessment.

How Can Organizations Avoid POA&M and OPA Failures During CMMC Certification?

Knowing what belongs in a POA&M versus an OPA is the first step. Building them with the specificity, evidence and structure that will hold up under a C3PAO assessment is the harder one. GuidePoint Security CMMC Readiness Assessment and Advisory Services can help your organizations at every stage of the CMMC journey, from scoping and gap assessments through documentation, remediation and assessment readiness. Organizations that go through the process walk into their assessment with clean documentation, defensible evidence and a clear understanding of where they stand.

FAQs

What happens if a POA&M is not closed within 180 days?

The organization loses its conditional CMMC certification status. The C3PAO must verify closure before final certification is granted. There is no extension process.

When should an organization use an OPA instead of standard vulnerability management?

An OPA applies when a temporary deficiency falls outside routine patching or scanning cycles. Standard vulnerability management under RA.L2-3.11.3 handles known, recurring issues. Use an OPA for gaps that need a documented mitigation plan.

Why do organizations fail POA&M reviews during CMMC assessments?

Most failures stem from documentation gaps, not security gaps. Organizations submit vague timelines, omit mitigation details or reuse pre-CMMC implementation plans. Assessors expect specific dates, responsible parties and evidence of progress.

Do subcontractors need their own POA&M for CMMC?

Yes. Each organization seeking CMMC certification must maintain its own POA&M. Subcontractors cannot rely on a prime contractor’s documentation.

What happens if a vulnerability is found after a CMMC assessment?

Post-assessment vulnerabilities are tracked through an OPA, not a POA&M. The OPA documents the issue and mitigation plan without triggering a new assessment cycle.

Title: CISA Expands Incident Reporting Form While CIRCIA Mandate Waits
Context: More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat
Full Text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has rolled out a revamped cyber incident reporting form that asks more granular questions about incident types and frames observed activity in MITRE ATT&CK terms.

CISA outlined the changes in an announcement published November 9 and the updated web-based questionnaire is available through its Incident Reporting Portal.

The agency said better data quality will help it connect related threat activity into broader trends that would otherwise look like separate incidents. The update draws on community feedback CISA has received over the years.

More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms

The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Questions about observed activity now use MITRE ATT&CK, a framework for describing adversary behavior that CISA said is familiar to the cyber community.

The changes are meant to support rapid but thorough threat analysis, according to CISA.

"In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization's detection is another's protection," said Chris Butera, CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity. "As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation's collective defense."

For now, only federal civilian agencies are required to report incidents to CISA. The agency encouraged other organizations that experience an incident to report voluntarily, and information they submit can be protected from disclosure under the Protected Critical Infrastructure Information (PCII) Program.

CIRCIA Rule Remains at White House

The update comes as the final rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) awaits approval. The rule went to the White House for review on October 1 and remains listed as pending.

Read more on CIRCIA: US Critical Infrastructure Braces for Sweeping New Cyber Reporting Rules

Once the rule takes effect, covered critical infrastructure organizations would have to report qualifying cyber incidents within 72 hours of reasonably believing they occurred and ransom payments within 24 hours of making them, according to CISA.

CISA published its proposed CIRCIA rule in April 2024 but missed an October 2025 statutory deadline to finalize it. Many comments on the proposal asked for a narrower scope, less burden and closer alignment with other federal reporting rules, according to CISA's regulatory agenda.

CISA's announcement did not mention CIRCIA or whether the enhanced reporting form would be used under the pending rule.

Title: Blind Eagle Uses Fake Court Notices to Deliver Remote Access Trojan Across Latin America
Context: Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-...
Full Text:
The threat actor known as Blind Eagle has resurfaced with a new campaign targeting organizations in Latin America through judicial and administrative-themed phishing lures to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) that shares its lineage with AsyncRAT and DCRat.

"The campaign uses Portuguese and Spanish lures that resemble court notifications, fiscalía notices, tutela proceedings, and administrative documents," Zenox said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

Assessed to be a Spanish-speaking group and active since 2018, Blind Eagle (aka APT-C-36) has a track record of using spear-phishing lures to distribute commodity RATs like AsyncRAT, BitRAT, Lime RAT, NjRAT, Quasar RAT, and Remcos RAT.

Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-laced attachment.

One email containing a Colombian judicial-themed XHTML file has been identified as a weaponized Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) image that renders a bogus web page impersonating Colombia's Fiscalía General de la Nación, also referred to as the Office of the Attorney General.

The web page, for its part, employs a technique known as HTML smuggling to assemble the next-stage ZIP archive payload locally in the web browser using ZipCrypto, thereby circumventing email security controls.

Present within the ZIP archive is a JavaScript dropper that masquerades as Network Configuration Auditor version 2.7.298. The JavaScript code conducts environment reconnaissance, and collects details such as system version, network profile, installation date, memory size, computer name, environment variables, and directories localized in Portuguese and Spanish.

Upon execution, it launches a Visual Basic Script that performs Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypass, while displaying a fake criminal-citation page as a distraction mechanism.

In parallel, the malware also takes steps to delete the original XHTML artifact, clears Mark of the Web (MotW) metadata, and sets up persistence on the host under the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically executed on system startup.

The attack culminates with the use of PowerShell to decode and launch the final RAT payload in memory. The trojan is an AsyncRAT fork with DCRat lineage based on code structure, configuration, build characteristics, and observed behavior.

"The targeting of judicial, fiscal, administrative and educational organizations gives the operation access to highly sensitive legal, financial and institutional information," Zenox said.

"Combined with the Portuguese and Spanish lures, Brazilian infrastructure, operational timezone and regional victimology, these elements establish the campaign as an APT-C-36 operation conducted through a Brazilian operational cluster."

Zenox told The Hacker News that it could not confirm whether any of these attacks had succeeded against real-world targets. However, during the campaign period between late October and early November 2026, it observed a large-scale wave of targeted phishing involving nearly 3,300 malicious emails.

While not all of these messages targeted organizations in Colombia, the country continues to remain a priority target for Blind Eagle for a combination of reasons.

"The repeated targeting of Colombia likely reflects multiple factors, with one of the main enabling factors being the structural vulnerabilities and uneven security maturity across parts of the country's critical, public, financial, and private-sector infrastructure," Zenox security researcher Gabriel Alves said.

"These conditions may increase the likelihood of successful compromises and offer greater opportunities to monetize access, steal sensitive data or funds, or reuse compromised credentials against critical systems. This is further supported by regional actors' familiarity with the Colombian context and is consistent with patterns observed among Latin American threat actors."

(The story was updated after publication to include additional insights from Zenox.)

Title: Russia-Linked Turla Hijacks Exchange Servers to Spy on NATO and EU Emails
Context: "On a compromised Exchange server, the most interesting activity is not always the message that arrives in a user's inbox," wrote Matias Porolli, the ESET researcher who...
Full Text:
Russia-linked threat group Turla has deployed a new toolset called Cereal on compromised government Microsoft Exchange servers, in one case setting it to pick out emails sent to or from NATO and European Union addresses.

ESET has attributed Cereal with high confidence to Turla, also known as Snake and Uroburos, in research published November 10. The group has been active since at least 2004 and is widely assessed to be part of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB).

The security company identified two national government victims, one in Kazakhstan and one in Romania. It found no external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure: each compromised Exchange server was co-opted to act as the C2 instead.

Cereal Turned Exchange Into a Collection Point

ESET wrote that the toolset was designed to take commands, run them in memory, map the compromised organization and gather selected messages through a new Exchange email collection module.

Cereal kept its payloads encrypted, received commands as separate .NET assemblies and ran the email collection module inside Exchange's own processes. According to ESET, the toolset paired techniques demanding a deep understanding of Exchange internals with unusual .NET execution methods.

"On a compromised Exchange server, the most interesting activity is not always the message that arrives in a user's inbox," wrote Matias Porolli, the ESET researcher who discovered the threat.

ESET's research does not describe how the servers were first compromised, but its white paper and GitHub repository list indicators of compromise.

Government Victims Matched Turla's Regional Focus

Cereal was set to pick out NATO and EU emails at the Romanian victim, found a month after ESET first spotted the toolset in Kazakhstan on November 28, 2025.

ESET wrote that this focus fits long-standing Russian intelligence priorities but may also relate to regional tensions, including Russian drones crashing near or inside Romania since early 2025. For Kazakhstan, it pointed to reported deportations of some Russian exiles since January 2026, suggesting operators may want visibility into Russian dissidents.

Around 70% of the countries Turla has targeted since 2022 have been former Soviet republics or European states once closely aligned with the Soviet Union, based on ESET telemetry.

Read more on Turla: Palo Alto Reveals New Features in Russian APT Turla's Kazuar Backdoor

Cereal was built for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage, ESET concluded. In its assessment, the victims' Exchange servers became collection points, internal execution hubs and cover for Turla's .NET tradecraft, with little left on disk to find.

Google Calendar Phishing Attacks Target Corporate Users

Researchers at Material Security warn that phishing attacks are harvesting live Google sessions from corporate users and bypassing multifactor authentication.

"The messages arrive as Google Calendar invites, sometimes delivered by BCC and often sent from an organization the recipient has already corresponded with," the researchers write. "The pretexts are mundane: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices. Most links point to Google itself.

"The typical pattern is Google's own /url redirector with the real destination in a query parameter, though other waves used share[.]google and Drive file links for the same purpose. One variant used Intuit transaction notification links. In every case, when the message is scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation displayed are legitimate and trusted."

The attacks are designed to harvest a range of multifactor authentication codes, enabling the threat actors to immediately gain access to the victims' accounts. "The attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the genuine Google sign-in page," the researchers explain. "The victim enters a password, receives a real prompt, and approves it, all while the operator watches the session in real time.

"The server relays SMS codes, authenticator codes, Google's Tap-Yes number matching, and phone-based account recovery to Google as each one arrives, so none of the second-factor controls stop the session from being captured."

Material disrupted the attackers' infrastructure, and this particular campaign has been shut down. The researchers stress, however, that the threat actors will most likely set up new infrastructure to continue launching attacks.

"Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, the framework has been public since February, and the operator shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code," the researchers write. "The branch includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt.

"None of those paths resolve today, and adding the brand requires dropping in a file rather than changing any code. The operator has built the follow-on and has not activated it. Material reads the theme rotation as iteration, not retirement, and expects the next pivot to look much like this one with a different brand."

Title: France Blames Iran for Supermarket Fridge Hack, Requests International Arrest Warrants
Context: Laure Beccuau, the Paris Public Prosecutor, said on social media the investigation found links between the October 11 to 12 cyber-attack and the Shahid Kaveh and Shahid...
Full Text:
The recent wave of cyber-attacks targeting refrigeration control systems across 700 supermarkets sites in France was coordinated by Iranian hacking groups, according to French authorities.

Laure Beccuau, the Paris Public Prosecutor, said on social media the investigation found links between the October 11 to 12 cyber-attack and the Shahid Kaveh and Shahid Shoostari groups, two elite offensive cyber units tied to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

In a technical attribution notice published on November 9, the French Computer Emergency and Response Team (CERT-FR) said Shahid Kaveh is linked to a range of purported hacktivist groups, including CyberAveng3rs, Soldiers of Solomon, Mr. Soul and Cyber Isnaad Front.

Investigators from the Anti-Criminality Office (OFAC) and the French domestic intelligence service (DGSI) found IP addresses linked to Iran-based endpoints and observed Farsi words in the traces left by the hackers.

Additionally, the techniques, tactics and procedures (TTPs) employed by the attackers were consistent with previous Shahid Kaveh campaigns.

CERT-FR named three leaders of the IRGC and Shahid Kaveh linked to the cyber-attacks.

The Paris prosecutor's office has now opened a judicial investigation into the cyber-attacks and the damage caused.

France Vows to Take Punitive Measures

According to another statement issued by the French government on November 9, Paris intends to take a series of diplomatic and punitive measures in response to the cyber-attacks.

The government announced that it would summon Iran’s Ambassador to France to formally convey its strongest condemnation of the attacks.

It also stated that it would urge its European partners to introduce additional sanctions targeting Iranian individuals and entities allegedly involved in the cyber-attacks against France, as well as other malicious cyber activities.

The French government stressed that it reserves the right to take further measures, both public and undisclosed, should they be deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to the cyber threats.

Frist Nation-State, Sabotage-Focused Cyber-Attack on French Soil

Historically, France has rarely attributed cyber-attacks to a single country, making this move particularly significant.

“This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, marking the first cyber-offensive campaign carried out purely for sabotage purposes on French national territory,” the French government explained in its statement.

Commenting on the attribution, Gary Barlet, public sector CTO at Illumio, said he is also “impressed” that France is planning to pursue sanctions at a European level.

“It's not yet clear what form those sanctions will take, so that will be interesting to see. But this needs to happen more often. Too often an attack gets publicly called out, there's outrage, and then nothing happens. It sends a message to attackers that the cost of doing this is close to zero,” Barlet added.

In the CERT-FR technical notice, the French Cyber Crises Coordination Center (C4) said this attack added to a series of other incidents that have been attributed to IRGC-linked groups since at least 2020. These include destabilisation campaigns targeting satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and a French digital display company in 2024, in the context of the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

This attribution does not include the cyber-attack on the French Blood Service (EFS) that occurred in early November.

Following recent cyber attacks on French blood banks and European supermarkets, U.S. federal agencies are urging critical infrastructure organizations to immediately secure industrial refrigeration systems against remote tampering and temperature manipulation.

Key takeaways

Cybercriminals are actively targeting unpatched flaws, misconfigurations, and weak or hard-coded passwords in commercial cold-chain and refrigeration controllers globally.

Attackers are gaining remote access to manipulate temperature controls and spoil essential products, such as blood and food.

CISA, the FBI, and other U.S. agencies are advising organizations to isolate OT systems, secure or remove remote access, patch critical vulnerabilities, and replace end-of-life devices.

Critical infrastructure organizations in the healthcare, chemicals, transportation, and food and agriculture sectors must urgently harden their industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems to protect food, medicines, and other essential products against ongoing cyber attacks.

That’s the call from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and other U.S. government agencies, following a series of alarming breaches against refrigeration systems in French blood banks and European supermarkets.

“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” CISA Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera said in a statement.

Attackers are remotely targeting electronic-temperature and commercial-refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. They’re looking for unpatched vulnerabilities and other security flaws, such as misconfigurations, according to the agencies.

Once attackers gain remote access to these systems, they try to tamper with these machines’ temperature controls to damage their refrigerated products. The temperature changes could also trigger fire hazards.

In a joint fact sheet, the agencies recommend organizations immediately take the following steps:

Use strong authentication mechanisms and change systems’ default passwords.

Keep systems updated and promptly patch critical vulnerabilities.

Replace legacy devices that have reached end-of-life status.

Identify systems accessible from the internet.

Isolate operational technology (OT) systems from business networks.

Remove unnecessary remote access.

Secure necessary remote access.

Maintain offsite backups.

“This fact sheet provides clear, practical steps that network defenders can take to reduce that risk and protect operations,” said Brett Leatherman, cyber branch operations director at the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), one of the authoring agencies.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the U.S. Department of Transportation (DoT) also contributed to the joint fact sheet.

Attackers hit hundreds of grocery stores in France several weeks ago that caused food to spoil and triggered fires. The National Cybersecurity Agency of France (ANSSI) recently told Cybersecurity Dive it has been investigating the attacks since they started in mid-October and is aware of compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series controllers, as well as Copeland and Dixell XWEB controllers.

In this article

California wants to switch off autoplay and personalized feeds for under-16s.

Google, Meta, and TikTok are suing to stop the restrictions.

Age checks could raise privacy concerns for adults, too.

Google, Meta, and TikTok filed separate federal lawsuits on November 4, challenging Assembly Bill 1709, which Governor Gavin Newsom signed in September.

The companies argue that the law, due to take effect in 2027, interferes with free speech, overrides parents’ decisions, and conflicts with federal protections for online platforms.

AB 1709 prohibits covered platforms from providing California users under 16 certain

“psychologically exploitative features intended to maximize engagement that foreseeably lead to compulsive use.”

The law specifically includes personalized “addictive feeds” and autoplay. It also allows the attorney general to define additional features through regulations.

It would not ban children from using the platforms. They can keep their accounts if the platform removes the restricted features. Otherwise, the platform must delete the account and associated personal information.

The law also requires age verification before providing the restricted features. The law doesn’t stop children from searching for videos, following creators, or communicating privately. It makes exceptions for certain search-based results, content that a user explicitly requests, and direct private messages, subject to conditions.

California’s argument is that harm is not limited to what children see. It can also arise from how a service encourages them to keep using it, through personalized recommendations and features such as autoplay.

The idea behind the law is straightforward: Instead of relying entirely on teenagers to recognize when to stop, require platforms to remove some of the mechanisms designed to keep them engaged.

The companies’ objections

The companies’ objections fall into several related categories.

Meta argues that deciding which posts to show, and how to arrange them, is protected editorial judgment under the First Amendment. Its complaint accuses California of attempting to appoint itself the

“editor, curator, and controller of online speech.”

TikTok makes a similar argument about its For You feed. It says selecting and arranging videos creates a curated product protected by free-speech rights, not merely a mechanism that the state can redesign at will.

Google likewise argues that YouTube’s recommendations help users find relevant, appropriate material among its vast collection of videos. It also defends autoplay as useful for watching content intended to be viewed in sequence.

The central disagreement is whether these are harmful product features that California can regulate, or editorial decisions protected by free-speech rights. California describes them as potentially harmful product design; the companies describe them as protected decisions about publishing speech.

The companies also raise parental control. Google says parents are best placed to decide what is appropriate for their families. TikTok points to its existing teen-account safeguards and Family Pairing controls, arguing that the law restricts free expression while taking decisions away from parents. Meta adds that personalized features can help deliver age-appropriate experiences.

The business model

There is also a commercial interest at stake: engagement. How often people return, how long they stay, and how much they interact all matter to the platforms’ businesses.

Meta’s annual report says it generates substantially all its revenue from advertising. It also says that changes to its content displays and product features can affect time spent, user engagement, and financial results. That doesn’t establish why the companies sued, but it helps explain why restrictions on recommendations and autoplay could have financial consequences.

If removing these features leads people to spend less time on a service, it could mean fewer opportunities to show ads. Compliance would also require product and operational changes, such as checking users’ ages and providing a different experience to those under 16.

Youth is the future. Big Tech is very much aware of this. Meta’s annual report identifies youth as an investment priority and describes attracting and retaining users as a competitive objective. Restrictions affecting how young people join and use a platform could affect its longer-term audience strategy, too.

What the future will bring

California is challenging an important part of the attention-based business model. Meta’s annual report warns investors that regulation affecting how it displays content or serves younger users could affect user growth, engagement, and financial results.

And then there’s the matter of age verification. The required age checks could affect adults as well as children: a service must verify users’ ages before providing the restricted features. Depending on how the checks work, this could involve sharing age-related information, raising privacy concerns and creating another opportunity for sensitive data to be exposed in a breach.

If it were up to me, platforms would stop designing for compulsive use, whatever the user’s age. Adults deserve a healthier online experience too. Applying those protections to everyone would also remove the need to check someone’s age before deciding whether they can use these features. Platforms might lose some advertising opportunities, but time spent online should not be the only measure of a successful service.

Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once.

Title: CISA, FBI Urge Action to Protect Industrial Refrigeration Networks
Context: The US government has urged organizations to take action to protect refrigeration systems from attacks that seek to remotely alter settings, including temperatures
Full Text:
The US government has urged organizations to take action to protect refrigeration systems from attacks that seek to remotely alter settings, including temperatures.

The advisory, issued by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the FBI and other federal agencies, said that US authorities “are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally.”

The warning follows a number of recent incidents in which hackers accessed internet-connected refrigeration systems and have attempted to tamper with temperatures.

Such attacks can have had huge real-world impacts, including ruining food and medical supplies.

On October 11, 2026, it was reported that several supermarket chains in France and other countries in Europe were forced to destroy food stock after hackers compromised systems administered by refrigeration systems provider Danfoss. The attackers reportedly programmed systems to reach temperatures as high as 50 °C (122°F).

A similar incident occurred on November 1, with supermarkets in at least nine European countries reportedly impacted.

Most recently, a cyber-attack targeting refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld saw cold storage rooms in France's National Blood Service (EFS) turned to a boiling temperature of 110°C (230°F).

The US advisory, published on November 5, warned operators and owners of refrigeration systems in the US to be vigilant for similar attacks.

This is particularly in sectors such as healthcare, chemical, food and agriculture, and transportation, which widely use these systems for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management and energy optimization.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the authoring agencies wrote.

They noted that hackers can use techniques like authentication bypass, arbitrary code injection and weak configurations to gain remote access to these internet-exposed systems.

Urgent Action Required to Protect Refrigeration Systems

The authoring agencies set out a number of immediate actions security teams should take to mitigate risks to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, based on the recent threats observed. These include:

Ensure control system devices, particularly controller panels are not exposed to the internet

Should remote access be necessary, protect these systems using a firewall or edge device and update them to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities

Isolate operational technology devices from business networks

Change default passwords and implement strong authentication policies, including phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA)

Establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire and replace legacy devices that are end of life

Limit access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes

Maintain backup systems offsite and offline and regularly test them

CISA’s acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity Chris Butera, commented: “Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target. We urge you to review the joint fact sheet and take action now to close known security gaps.”

Refrigeration Systems Taken Offline Following Europe Incidents

Data published by Censys on November 5 revealed there has been a 53% reduction in internet-exposed refrigeration controllers across the Danfoss StoreView and Copeland/Dixell XWEB products that were compromised during the supermarket incidents on October 11 and November 2, respectively.

The big fall in exposure is consistent with provider action or owners disconnecting devices, Censys noted.

So far, the incidents have not been attributed to a particular threat actor.

Title: The White House is apparently a popular residential proxy exit spot
Context: The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose...
Full Text: Whether through malware or other means, devices associated with the White House network appear to be serving as residential proxy exit nodes, potentially posing security risks to one of the world's most sensitive networks. News of the security snafu comes from security firm Layer3 Intel, which reported this week that it discovered the likely illicit activity thanks to its recently launched Residential Proxy Observatory. According to Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk, the White House residential proxy activity might have gone unnoticed if not for the new tool. “The observatory is just a public interface to explore the data we've been collecting for the past year,” Usatyuk told The Register in an email. For those unfamiliar with residential proxies, they're like any old proxy network that obfuscates the location of a user, except in this case their exit nodes use IP addresses associated with residential internet connections, as opposed to datacenters. While many are legitimate, others are exploited by threat actors and used in the commission of cybercrimes, as the FBI warned earlier this year. The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose user computers as exit nodes, and other threats used to turn victims into nodes without their consent. Residential proxies are commonly used by threat actors to conceal command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, conduct phishing attacks, send spam, disguise malicious traffic, and the like, the FBI explained. According to Layer3, its data shows 28 distinct residential proxy services exiting into the White House network nearly every day between October 5 and November 3, with 236 separate exits in that period. Other residential proxy detection services logged the same information, Layer3 said. Most of the activity was happening in the evening, White House time, between 5 pm and midnight. That, Layer3 said, suggests someone at the White House - not a guest - has an infected device that’s serving as an exit, likely via an infected proxy SDK. If correct, that’s a problem. “Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement,” Layer3 explained. “If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.” In other words, this is a serious security risk, and one Usatyuk tells us could have been a problem for a while. “Our data retention period goes back to July 10,” the Layer3 founder explained. “Given that there was continuous activity for a matter of months and other res proxy detection services independently verified the data, it's likely that White House IPs have been used by res proxy networks for all sorts of activity for some time now.” Usatyuk said his firm’s data isn’t detailed enough to know how many machines are being used as exit nodes inside the White House network. He pointed us to an X post from security firm Synthient, which said it believes there are multiple Windows 10 and 11 devices on the White House network that likely have the Infatica SDK installed on them. Infatica offers a software development kit (SDK) that allows app developers to monetize users' internet connections by turning their devices into residential proxy exit nodes. The possibility that this software is running on devices associated with the White House network raises serious security concerns: Vulnerable proxy software could potentially provide attackers with a route into internal systems. Usatyuk told us that the most recent residential proxy activity on the White House network occurred Wednesday night, “hours after the blog went live,” but has since stopped. The US State Department contacted Layer3 Thursday morning to request a copy of the company’s logs, which Usatyuk tells us he’s sent over. “Hopefully they've figured out the situation,” Usatyuk added - and hopefully before any government secrets have been exposed. The White House didn't respond to questions for this story.®

Title: October crypto-tracker hack: Access cracked, law enforcement tokens packed
Context: In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of...
Full Text: Blockchain analysis outfit Chainalysis has confirmed that when attackers broke into its systems in October, they managed to grab usernames, password hashes, and live tokens. In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of the attack for the first time. In previous updates, which Chainalysis has issued regularly since it detected the intrusion on October 30, it confirmed that user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels were exposed. The news of password hashes and live tokens also being accessed reflects a worsening picture for the company. Chainalysis did not confirm the type of hashing algorithm it used to encrypt users' passwords, which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about the offline crackability of users' hashed credentials. Some users received emails instructing them to change their passwords, but Chainalysis said in its latest update that the password reset functionality is currently down. Nevertheless, users were also encouraged to change their passwords on any site where they reuse credentials. In addition to the exposed data, Chainalysis also detected "abnormal activity" on its transaction screening products, and has taken services down while "our team completes critical work." These include, but are not limited to, the Reactor blockchain investigation platform used by international law enforcement customers, the Data Solutions threat intelligence platform, and the KYT (know your transaction) anti-money laundering solution's user interface and login page. Regarding Reactor and the associated investigation data, Chainalysis said: "At this time, we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated." The company plans to reinstate KYT and the risk-intelligence Address Screening tool at some point today (Thursday November 5). Customers will have to provide the company’s support team or their account manager with trusted IP addresses, which will be added to an allowlist. From there, users can begin resetting their passwords. "We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online," Chainalysis said. "We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary. "We know how business-critical these services are to our customers, and we are working expeditiously alongside our outside experts to restore them securely." Chainalysis has not yet commented on who was behind the attack, but implied that the culprits used an AI agent, and likened the attack to others that have hit "many other tech platforms in recent weeks." "This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," it told customers in its initial disclosure on October 30. "Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems." In Wednesday's updates, it referred to the intrusion as an "ongoing multifront cyberattack," and later, an "on-path attack," otherwise known as an attacker-in-the-middle (AitM) attack, without elaborating further about what it entailed. Per its own company description, Chainalysis counts government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, financial institutions, and cybersecurity companies among its customer base. It is one of the world's foremost blockchain analysis companies and is routinely engaged to assist in cyber-related law enforcement investigations. Recent cases the company was asked to support include the takedowns of crypto-laundering network AudiA6 and bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine, both of which were known facilitators of ransomware crews. It also played a role in bringing down the infamous LockBit ransomware operation, among other engagements in the interim. ®

Title: Residential Proxy Traffic Traced to White House Network
Context: Layer3 Intel, a New York-based residential proxy detection firm, detailed the findings in research published on November 4
Full Text:
Residential proxy traffic has exited through the White House network 236 times over a 30-day period, with 28 separate residential proxy services able to route traffic through six of its addresses.

Layer3 Intel, a New York-based residential proxy detection firm, detailed the findings in research published on November 4. Residential proxies are services that sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from each device's network.

The addresses sit in AS2650, the block of internet addresses (autonomous system) registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Layer3 spotted the exits, recorded on 26 of the 30 days between October 5 and November 3, in its newly launched Residential Proxy Observatory.

Layer3 cross-checked the addresses against public lookup pages from proxy detection services Spur and Synthient, which independently identified them as residential proxy exits.

Evening Pattern Suggests a Single Device

Layer3 said anyone could route traffic out through the same addresses by signing up to a public residential proxy service and paying a few dollars. It found the activity by chance, while requesting ordinary global rotating access through these services.

About half of the activity fell between 5pm and midnight Eastern Time, with almost none in the early morning.

Layer3 said that pattern suggested a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device was infected with a proxy software development kit (SDK).

"Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them," the firm wrote.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk said: “The most recent activity was recorded in the evening of November 4; hopefully, it stops soon!”

Read more on residential proxy networks: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet

No Compromise Reported, but Proxy SDKs Carry Risk

Layer3 did not report any compromise of White House systems. It said it has backed up the raw logs of the activity and has shared their finfings with a US federal agency.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow access to internal networks and lateral movement, which is how past botnets have spread.

Layer3 cited Synthient research showing the Kimwolf botnet reached at least two million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed Android Debug Bridge (ADB) service, through residential proxy networks.

If an SDK on the White House network had the same kind of flaw, Layer3 said, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

Infosecurity has contacted the White House for comment.

Title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
Context: In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local...
Full Text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

Title: The Race Against the 3-Day Clock: How Rapid7 Helps Meet BOD 26-04 Compliance
Context: The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were...
Full Text:
Introduction to BOD 26-04

On June 10, 2026, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk." Strip away the regulatory language and it reads like a single operational fact: for a vulnerability that is actively exploited, publicly reachable, and grants an attacker full control, you now have three calendar days to remediate it — and you must run a forensic investigation in parallel to determine whether you've already been breached.

The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, down from 38% the year before. That's a 43-day reality vs. a 3-day mandate; a gap you don't exactly just close by hiring more workers.

This blog aims to break down what BOD 26-04 actually requires, mapping each point to the Rapid7 capability that helps to make compliance operationally achievable for all.

What did CISA actually change?

BOD 26-04 supersedes and revokes two prior directives: BOD 19-02 (2019), which prioritized internet-facing vulnerabilities by static CVSS score, and BOD 22-01 (2021), which created the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog but applied a 14-day patch deadline to every entry regardless of context.

Note that flat timeline: under BOD 22-01, an actively exploited bug on an air-gapped internal server carried the same 14-day urgency as one on a public-facing web server granting full admin control. Teams burned cycles patching low-risk systems to satisfy a checklist. BOD 26-04 replaces that with a dynamic model: prioritize what attackers are actually exploiting, and formally defer what they aren't.

The four variables to BOD 26-04

BOD 26-04 abandons CVSS as the sole trigger and evaluates every vulnerability against four binary variables, derived from the SSVC decision framework (CMU CERT/CC and CISA):

Asset Exposure: Is the asset reachable by untrusted entities over a public network?

KEV Status: Is the CVE on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog?

Exploit Automation: Can an attacker automate the full exploit chain, enabling mass exploitation?

Technical Impact: Does successful exploitation grant Total control (arbitrary code execution, full/admin privileges) or only Partial control (limited access, information exposure, denial of service)?

Asset exposure is the highest-leverage variable. If you remove an asset from public reach, you flip the exposure variable from Yes to No, and the required timeline relaxes accordingly. Rapid7 Labs data underscores why exposure dominates: half of the vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild in Q1 2026 were zero-click, network-facing issues requiring no authentication, and by Q2 2026 nearly two-thirds required no user interaction at all. Attackers are going straight at exposed, unauthenticated surfaces.

CISA's new remediation tiers

The four variables combine into a graduated timeline (CISA BOD 26-04, Appendix A, Table 1). The tiers, simplified:

Tier

Timeline

Core criteria

1 (Critical)

3 days + forensic triage

On KEV and Total control

2 (High)

3 days (no triage)

Publicly exposed + Automatable + Total control, not yet on KEV

3 (Accelerated)

14 days

KEV-listed without Total control; or exposed + Partial control

4 (Standard)

60 days

Internal, automatable, Partial control

5 (Deferred)

Fix on next system upgrade

Internal + not KEV + not automatable + Partial control

Note that these timelines are dynamic. If a dormant vulnerability is added to the KEV, its clock can compress from 60 days to 3 overnight. Conversely, if you isolate an exposed asset, its clock relaxes. CISA explicitly counts isolation, mitigation, and uninstalling the vulnerable software as valid remediation; as such, a compensating control is a legitimate, compliant way to buy time for a safe patch.

The forensic triage mandate

This is the first of the requirements to have no precedent in earlier directives. For Tier 1 vulnerabilities (KEV + Total control), you must not only patch within three days, but run a concurrent forensic investigation to determine whether the asset is already compromised. Why? When an attacker exploits an exposed edge device, they establish persistence within hours; thus, patching three days later closes the door with the intruder already inside.

CISA's implementation guidance lays out a six-step, 72-hour protocol:

Phase

Window

What happens

1. Scoping

0–2 hrs

Identify in-scope devices; activate response team; open out-of-band comms

2. Preserve evidence

2–24 hrs

Capture volatile data (RAM, cache, registries) before any change

3. Patch & stabilize

2–24 hrs

Apply patches only after evidence is collected

4. Contain

6–24 hrs

Isolate infrastructure without tipping off the attacker

5. Triage analysis

24–48 hrs

Hunt IOCs; look for lateral movement and data staging

6. Escalation decision

48–72 hrs

Formal report; if compromised, report to CISA and pivot to full IR

Note the built-in tension between Step 2 and Step 3: patching reboots systems and overwrites the exact volatile memory that proves or disproves a compromise. You have to capture forensic evidence before you patch — at speed, across every affected endpoint. Doing that manually inside 72 hours is not always realistic.

Who CISA's BOD 26-04 applies to

BOD 26-04 is compulsory for all Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies. It excludes national security systems and DoD/Intelligence Community systems.

It reaches the private sector indirectly, but firmly. Agencies must review contracts and push compliance onto supply-chain partners. For FedRAMP and cloud offerings, agencies stay responsible for their hosted systems' compliance, which forces CSPs handling federal data to adopt the same 3-day triage standard. If you're a contractor or CSP touching federal data, treat this as your standard too.

Mapping Rapid7 to the directive

Meeting a 3-day clock with mandatory forensics is impossible through manual process. Here's how the Rapid7 Command Platform maps to each requirement.

Variable 1 (Exposure) → Surface Command

You can't calculate a timeline if you don't know what's exposed. Surface Command combines Cyber Asset Attack Surface Management (CAASM) with External Attack Surface Management (EASM), correlating continuous external scanning against an internal asset inventory ingested from your existing tools. The result is a single view of your true external attack surface — including the shadow IT attackers can see but your team can't. When it flags an exposed asset carrying a KEV-listed CVE, you can sever exposure to flip Variable 1 and de-escalate the timeline while you test the patch.

Variables 2 & 3 (KEV + Automation) → InsightVM and Active Risk

InsightVM tracks the KEV Catalog natively in its Threat Feed Dashboard, continuously updating which assets carry actively targeted vulnerabilities. Its Active Risk score — a 0–1,000 scale — moves beyond static CVSS by ingesting exploit intelligence from Metasploit, ExploitDB, the CISA KEV list, and Rapid7 Labs research. That mirrors the directive's own logic: a CVSS 7.5 bug with a weaponized Metasploit module will outrank a CVSS 9.8 bug with no known exploit — exactly the prioritization BOD 26-04 demands.

The NVD scoring gap → Exposure Command AI CVSS

The National Vulnerability Database can't keep pace with disclosure volume, leaving many CVEs unscored — a blind spot when a zero-day drops and you need a timeline immediately. Exposure Command fills it with an AI model trained on historical NVD data. On its own the model returns the correct severity classification 76% of the time; combined with Active Risk, that rises to 87%, with any miss never more than one classification off. Exposure Command also enriches every asset with business criticality and threat telemetry, and its Remediation Hub surfaces the fixes that cut the most risk.

The forensic mandate → Velociraptor

Velociraptor — the open-source DFIR project Rapid7 acquired in April 2021 — is built for exactly the scale and speed the triage mandate requires. It maps directly to the protocol: agents capture volatile memory and running-process data across thousands of endpoints simultaneously (Step 2), and analysts use Velociraptor Query Language to hunt CISA-provided IOCs enterprise-wide in real time, returning only relevant artifacts instead of pulling full disk images over the network (Step 5). That lets you satisfy the evidentiary requirement without delaying the Step 3 patch.

From severity to dollars

BOD 26-04 shares a core idea with modern risk management: technical severity isn't business impact. A high CVSS score doesn't answer the board's question of "how likely is this to cost us?"

The FAIR framework closes that gap by expressing risk as expected annual loss: Annualized Loss Expectancy = Loss Event Frequency × Loss Magnitude

BOD 26-04 is effectively a mechanism for pinning down Loss Event Frequency: by isolating vulnerabilities that are exploited (KEV), reachable (exposure), and scalable (automation), it identifies the ones statistically most likely to become a loss event. Feed Active Risk into the frequency side and FAIR into the cost side, and you can brief leadership in the language of capital, not CVE IDs.

Rapid7 case studies in the wild

Recent discoveries from Rapid7 Intelligence show the top tier in action:

Vulnerability

Impact

Why it's Tier 1

Rapid7 action

Microsoft SharePoint (CVE-2026-55040 + CVE-2026-63520)

Chained, the two flaws yield unauthenticated RCE via JWT bypass, running commands as the SharePoint service account

Internet-facing + total control (via the chain) + added to KEV after in-the-wild exploitation

Palo Alto PAN-OS (CVE-2026-0300)

Authentication bypass enabling full takeover of remote-management endpoints

High-value management assets; total control; added to KEV August 2026

Checks shipped via content release; Velociraptor hunted endpoint artifacts to satisfy triage

What's next for federal agencies and contractors?

If you're an FCEB agency or a contractor or CSP handling federal data, the following three moves matter most:

Get exposure right. Everything downstream depends on knowing what's publicly reachable. Establish continuous external-plus-internal asset visibility now.

Wire KEV into prioritization, not a spreadsheet. The clock starts the moment CISA updates the catalog. Ingestion has to be automated and continuous.

Pre-stage forensics. Decide today how you'll capture volatile evidence across endpoints inside 72 hours. If that's a manual runbook, it will fail under a real Tier 1 event.

CISA BOD 26-04's bottom line

BOD 26-04 retires "patch everything" in favor of operational precision: remediate the actively exploited, exposed, high-impact vulnerabilities in 72 hours, prove whether you've already been breached, and defer the rest. Meeting it takes continuous asset discovery, live threat intelligence, context-aware prioritization, and forensics at scale — which is precisely the shape of the Rapid7 Platform. For federal agencies it's a mandate; for everyone else, it's the clearest blueprint yet for risk-based vulnerability management.

Title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
Context: Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware
Full Text:
Smashing the botnet

Google worked with several other organizations to disrupt the x.cpe network, including Japan’s National Police Agency, Synthient, and Trend Micro. Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware. It also went after command-and-control servers operated by Videostrong that were connected to other malware campaigns. Google estimates Videostrong has been cut off from about 10 million compromised devices.

This action should make the affected devices safe to use, but probably not as safe as they should be. Play Protect is still disabled, and the inert malware modules are still installed. Since they are loaded as system apps, users cannot easily remove them.

Synthient has published a list of 182 device model names known to be included in the botnet. Anyone who has purchased a MECOOL or white label Android TV box of unknown origin should check it. Trend Micro counted a total of 1,472,554 infected devices, somewhat higher than Google’s estimate. The overwhelming majority were in Brazil, Malaysia, Iraq, Mexico, and Taiwan, but tens of thousands were also online in the US, Germany, the UK, Australia, and Canada.

Google determined the operation was not the work of a rogue actor, so it has ended its relationship with Videostrong. The company, as well as any subsidiaries, will not be permitted to use Google’s Android apps and services.

Google also notes that it is updating its certification process to close the loophole that allowed Videostrong to operate its botnet on certified devices. Android is open source, though, and there are countless uncertified Android-based TV boxes out there. Videostrong could continue to sell malicious hardware under other brands without Google apps. But it would still have to rebuild its malware operation from scratch.
