Key Takeaways

FedRAMP authorization isn’t the finish line. Providers are expected to keep monitoring their security posture and give federal agencies the information they need for ongoing, risk-based decisions.

CISA’s BOD 26-04, issued on June 10, 2026, moves federal vulnerability management toward risk-based prioritization instead of a single fixed deadline for every finding.

FedRAMP has said the legacy monthly scan is no longer sufficient. Its new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rules become mandatory for certification on December 7, 2026.

Ask anyone who has taken a cloud service through the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) what the process feels like, and you’ll hear roughly the same story. Months of control documentation, a System Security Plan running hundreds of pages, a Third-Party Assessment Organization (3PAO) assessment that turns up gaps nobody saw coming, and finally an Authority to Operate (ATO) letter. What that story usually leaves out is that the letter isn’t the finish line. It’s where the real work starts.

Once a Cloud Service Offering is authorized, FedRAMP expects the provider to continue monitoring its security posture and keep feeding federal agencies the information they need to make ongoing, risk-based decisions. On June 10, 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) raised that bar again with Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04, and FedRAMP moved fast to bring its own rules with it.

The takeaway is fairly simple. Getting authorized was never the hard part. Proving, day after day, that your controls are still doing what they’re supposed to do is the hard part, and it’s the problem policy audit automation exists to solve.

Getting FedRAMP authorized is step one. Learn how to stay authorized.

Watch on Demand

Why Point-in-Time Compliance Stopped Working

FedRAMP used to run on a predictable cadence. Assess, authorize, submit monthly scans, repeat. That model has been cracking for a while now, and three things are driving it.

Vulnerability doesn’t just mean a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry anymore. Misconfigurations and control drift are squarely in scope now, so a clean scan can still be hiding a compliance failure.

Environments move faster than assessment cycles do. Cloud-native infrastructure can drift a dozen times a week, while monitoring reports still tend to go out monthly or quarterly.

Regulators have stopped accepting “we’ll catch it at the next audit.” Federal risk management is moving away from calendar-based reviews and toward real-time, exposure-based decisions.

CISA BOD 26-04, in Plain Terms

BOD 26-04, issued by CISA in June 2026, moved federal vulnerability expectations toward continuous, risk-based validation instead of a single fixed deadline applied to every finding. FedRAMP responded within days, confirming that the legacy monthly scan most Rev5 Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) still lean on for their compliance evidence isn’t going to hold up anymore, and setting December 7, 2026, as the date its new Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules become mandatory for certification. For compliance and audit teams, the practical read is simple. The evidence you hand to an assessor has to reflect what’s true right now, not what was true at the last scan.

The Pain Points Teams Keep Naming

Talk to FedRAMP compliance teams, and the same challenges come up again and again:

Finding control gaps before an assessor does, instead of during the assessment window

Keeping configurations from drifting after they were compliant on day one

Prioritizing remediation when continuous assessment produces a continuous stream of findings

Providing continuous visibility instead of handing over a report generated the week before an audit

Producing audit-ready evidence on demand instead of assembling it after the fact

Cutting duplicate effort across overlapping frameworks, since most FedRAMP teams are also carrying National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53, Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC), Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and increasingly the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) on the same infrastructure

In PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey of 1,802 executives across 63 territories, 85% said compliance requirements have grown more complex over the last three years, and nearly 90% said the breadth of their compliance responsibilities has expanded over that same period. That pressure adds cost and strains the teams that have to prove compliance. Misconfigurations make it worse: Qualys analysis of more than 1 billion misconfiguration findings shows access control failures account for 38% of exposures, and organizations take an average of 14 months to fix these basic gaps.

None of this is a documentation problem. It’s an automation problem that’s been wearing a documentation costume.

How Policy Audit Solves the Problem

This is where a continuous assess, prioritize, remediate report workflow stops being a slide in a deck and starts being how the work actually gets done.

On the assessment side, instead of a monthly scan, Qualys Policy Audit continuously evaluates technical controls against the FedRAMP baseline, mapping each policy to a technical check, an expected value, and a pass or fail result across every system in scope. That’s the difference between documenting a control on paper and being able to prove it’s still operating the way it was the day you got your ATO.

Qualys lays this out as five practical steps rather than a single feature:

Connect findings to the control context. Connect raw findings to the control and framework context instead of handing teams a pile of technical output to interpret on their own.

Prioritize what impacts audit outcomes. This is where the volume problem gets solved. Research behind the approach found that fewer than 1% of vulnerabilities in a typical environment pose the highest risk or genuinely need immediate action to move audit outcomes, so results get filtered by control criticality, asset scope, internet-facing devices, the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, and risk signals like MITRE ATT&CK mappings, not just counted.

Automate remediation. Remediation is where the old workflow falls apart. Flag a finding, file a ticket, wait, hope someone remembers to re-scan. That process was never fast, and BOD 26-04’s tighter windows make it untenable. Audit Fix closes the loop instead, automating the fix itself and applying it consistently across assets rather than leaving it to a ticket queue.

Map controls across frameworks. A control validated once, whether that’s for FedRAMP, System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2, ISO 27001, General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), or something else, counts toward every other framework it maps to as well, so teams stop re-proving the same control for every audit that comes around.

Shift to continuous audit readiness. Audit outcomes should reflect the current state of the environment, not a snapshot from whenever someone last pulled a report. That’s the same point CISA and FedRAMP are making. For a closer look at each step, read 5 Steps to Turn Compliance Checks into Audit Outcomes.

Qualys Policy Audit doesn’t replace governance, training, or personnel security. Those stay organizational, and a configuration scanner can’t assess them. On the technical side, it assesses your systems against NIST 800-53 controls in families such as:

Configuration management (CM): settings checked against baselines, with drift flagged

System and information integrity (SI): integrity protections and file changes

Audit and accountability (AU): logging and audit settings

Risk assessment (RA): gaps ranked by risk, not just counted

Assessment, authorization, and monitoring (CA): continuous monitoring of control status

That’s not a coincidence. It’s the reason this category of tooling exists in the first place.

The Takeaway

FedRAMP compliance isn’t a project with an end date anymore. It’s an ongoing discipline, and the rules keep tightening. Teams that still treat authorization as the finish line keep getting caught off guard at reassessment. The teams staying ahead of directives like BOD 26-04, rather than scrambling to react to them, are the ones who’ve built assessing, prioritizing, remediating, and reporting into how they run compliance day-to-day, not just how they prepare for an audit.

If you want to see what that looks like, watch our on-demand webinar, “FedRAMP Authorization and What It Now Takes to Keep It.” It features Kaleb Knobel, Senior Security Analyst and Information System Security Officer (ISSO), and Anu Kapil, Director of Product Management. Why isn’t FedRAMP authorization the finish line?

After authorization, FedRAMP expects providers to keep monitoring their security posture and give agencies the information they need for ongoing, risk-based decisions. Proving that controls still work, day after day, is the harder part.

Base44 puts all of them in one workspace. With its new Compliance API, it also gives enterprise admins one place to govern them: who can open an app, who can read its data and who its agents can talk to.

Base44 just launched its Compliance API, and Orca is ready on day one. Today, Orca is extending AI AppGen Security to Base44. It joins Vercel and Claude in the same risk model and alert queue you already use for AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.

You can’t block your way out of AI outside your pipelines. You secure it through the platform’s control plane, then rank its risk against everything else you run.

Base44 built the controls. Orca keeps drift in check.

A single Base44 app now leaves a trail in three places: its settings live in Base44, its code can sync to GitHub, and the data it touches sits in your cloud. Each place has its own security view, and none of them shows the whole app. Security teams end up asking three tools one question: can this app put us at risk?

Base44’s enterprise controls are the foundation: SSO enforcement, SCIM, audit logs, IP allowlists, a Security Center that scans app code, and now a Compliance API that opens workspace settings to the rest of the security stack. Take two apps from the same well-governed workspace:

App A is a sales deal-tracking dashboard. It’s restricted to the workspace, each rep sees only their own records, and every admin uses MFA.

App B is an HR onboarding portal published last week. Its builder switched it to public for a vendor demo and never switched it back, so its Employees table is now readable without login.

From the outside, both are just URLs. Only the workspace configuration, now readable through Base44’s Compliance API, shows that App B drifted from policy.

The question isn’t “is anything misconfigured?”

It’s “which of these apps can actually create risk?”

Introducing the Orca Base44 connector

Title: NCSC Chief Warns of Imminent AI Ransomware Threat to UK Critical Infrastructure
Context: AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre...
Full Text:
AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned.

The country faces “a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” NCSC CEO Richard Horne said during the launch event for the agency’s annual State of the Cyber Nation report in London, on November 3.

Horne said this heightened threat is supercharged by the use of AI, whose impact “will be felt by us all, whether you and your organization choose to harness it or not.”

The report warned that AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in cyber-attacks conducted by financially motivated hackers against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028.

It also warned that nation states including Russia and China will routinely use AI in their cyber activity to achieve their geopolitical goals.

Yet, Horne emphasized that AI-based threats have not fundamentally revealed anything new.

The risk that looms is “not because AI has invented new ways to attack us,” he argued, but “because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.”

He pointed to “far too many organizations” relying on “tech on the cheap.”

“End-of-life systems kept running for just one more year, well-needed upgrades pushed back, as a 'cost efficiency' and technology providers failing to invest in security by design and default,” Horne outlined.

“We have installed technology then failed to invest in it throughout its lifecycle. Granted access where it was convenient rather than where it was necessary. Procured services based solely on their price without asking whether the technologies and operations underpinning them was resilient or secure. And failed to put in place the monitoring needed to detect when things go wrong,” he added.

UK Government Announces New Cybersecurity Investments

The best recent example, Horne said, is the threat of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. He noted that his agency has issued 110,000 proactive notifications and Early Warning alerts to UK organizations in response to the PHP vulnerabilities.

He also welcomed recent news that the British government has invested £60m ($80.4m) into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, including a £25m ($33.5m) Challenge Fund supporting UK AI and cyber security innovators, and £70m ($93.8m) for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.

These announcements, made on October 24, come alongside an additional £120m ($160.8m) investment in the AI Security Institute (AISI) and the establishment of new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the NCSC in Manchester to provide world leading AI security expertise within government.

The government has also committed £40m ($53.6m) to establishing a National Agentic Security Unit to monitor and respond to uncontrolled AI bots, alongside a further £24m ($32.1m) to strengthen public-sector cyber defenses using advanced AI technology.

Alongside these investments, Cyber Security Minister, Baroness Lloyd, announced in a speech at the NCSC Annual Review event that the UK government is offering a 75% discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small and medium-sized businesses, bringing the cost down to between £80 ($107) and £125 ($168), plus VAT.

More than 230 businesses have also signed up to the government's Cyber Resilience Pledge, which will allow participating organizations to refer SMEs in their supply chains for free Cyber Essentials certification, with selected businesses also receiving support from a free cyber security advisor.

The government also announced 14 new Software Security Ambassadors, including Fortinet, Thales, Capgemini and Zscaler, which will work with the government to promote secure software development and encourage wider adoption of its Software Security Code of Practice.

A “Moment of Choice” for UK Organizations

Horne said UK organizations and at “a moment of choice” and urged them to “reckon with the current state of their cybersecurity” as new technologies like AI will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead.

The NCSC report also suggested that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cybersecurity and that organizations must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber-attacks.

"We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency and where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all,” Horne said in his speech.

He added that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain, when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

Commenting on the report, Anthony Young, CEO at UK-based critical infrastructure security provider Bridewell, stressed that the NCSC’s two-year warning “feels generous.”

“AI is already helping attackers, and vulnerability discovery is accelerating faster than many organizations can test and deploy patches. There is no time to wait when so many of the weaknesses attackers can exploit are already there, highlighting the recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems are a good example of this and “an extension of the problems we have seen for years with internet-connected CCTV and heating or ventilation systems.”

“Organizations cannot assume that insurance will resolve the consequences of an attack when essential services are disrupted. Cyber Essentials matters because so many attacks still exploit basic weaknesses, and leaving those weaknesses in place makes life too easy for everyone from amateur hackers to nation-state attackers. We’ve spent 25 years telling organisations to get the basics right. AI is making it harder for them to get away with ignoring that advice,” Young added.

The warnings come as the UK government is taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defenses.

Title: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet
Context: “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving...
Full Text:
Google has banned a Chinese Android device maker and worked with partners to dismantle a botnet it helped to build containing more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, the tech giant has revealed.

In a blog post published on November 2, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it assessed “with high confidence” that Android ODM/OEM Videostrong Technology was responsible for the XCPE botnet and backdoor.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” it explained.

“These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices.”

Read more on botnets: Chinese Botnet Bypasses MFA in Microsoft 365 Attacks.

The industry action also disrupted XCPE command-and-control (C2) servers being used by criminal affiliates of Videostrong to install over a dozen malware families onto victims’ devices. This action helped to sever control of over 10 million of these compromised devices from the bot-herders, Google claimed.

“We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” the blog continued.

“We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

Aside from set-top boxes, the XCPE botnet included compromised telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

How XCPE Worked

Google claimed Videostrong had been selling devices with the XCPE backdoor embedded into the firmware for several years.

The backdoor itself, x.cpe, operated at android.uid.system privilege level and automatically reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition on reboot if a user tries to get rid of it.

On startup it contacts a C2 server and uses MQTT message broker for commands, enabling affiliates to remotely perform malicious actions such as executing shell scripts, disabling Google Play Protect, and silently installing additional apps.

Videostrong sought to further monetize the backdoor access to compromised devices by installing malware modules from other operators including residential proxy service providers like Linkfog, AppSalt/Honeygain, GaGaNode, NetNut and Traffmonetizer.

These are another popular enabler of cybercrime including account takeover, payment fraud, ad/click fraud, web scraping and DDoS.

"While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient,” Google warned in closing.

“Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry and the broader technology ecosystem.”

Title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
Context: A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co
Full Text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was endorsed in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linux Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Context: It's proof that collaboration is one of the most powerful tools we have against threats that cross borders and industries
Full Text:
Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Synthient and Japan's National Police Agency form coordinated effort combining security research, threat intelligence and network expertise to identify and disrupt X.CPE botnet

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, a group of private and public sector partners announced a coordinated takedown of X.CPE, a global botnet hidden in more than 1.3 million set-top boxes across more than 200 countries. Hidden on devices before they were ever sold, the botnet used subscribers' devices and home internet connections without their knowledge or consent. This takedown was led by Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security and Synthient, along with Japan's National Police Agency.

"Operations like this raise the cost for criminals and show that the infrastructure they rely on isn't out of reach," said Charley Snyder, Head of Disruption Operations at Google Threat Intelligence Group. "Disrupting X.CPE took partners across industry working together. It's proof that collaboration is one of the most powerful tools we have against threats that cross borders and industries."

A familiar device hiding an unfamiliar threat

X.CPE was embedded in firmware, the software that controls a device's basic operations, before set-top boxes reached subscribers' homes. X.CPE was built to evade pre-release security checks, and Google has since updated its review process in response, as well as banned the responsible OEM and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Unlike infections that depend on a user opening a suspicious attachment or installing an application, this threat arrived as part of the device itself. Subscribers received no consent request, notification or opt-out options.

Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Synthient, working with Japan's National Police Agency, carried out a coordinated disruption campaign against X.CPE. Each organization contributed in its own way, applying its expertise in connected-device security, malware analysis, network visibility and digital fraud to analyze the botnet and disrupt its operations.

Together they dismantled a threat hiding behind seemingly routine device activity: software embedded in TV set-top boxes that gave botnet controllers remote access and allowed them to exploit home broadband connections without subscriber consent. The takedown also disrupted the command-and-control domains that operate the criminal affiliates' malware modules. Because these affiliates distribute their modules through channels beyond X.CPE, Google assesses that taking down these domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

The effort demonstrates the importance of connecting intelligence across organizations to confront threats that cross technology and network boundaries. By bringing together distinct perspectives on compromised devices, malicious software and internet traffic, the partners supported a coordinated takedown aimed at disrupting unauthorized access and monetization and addressing risks to subscriber privacy, broadband resources and trust in connected devices.

Turning home broadband into a business without permission

The botnet generated revenue from compromised devices in a variety of ways, including: reselling bandwidth, delivering video content, ad fraud, loading additional backdoors and, in earlier versions, installing apps for payment.

Residential proxy software allowed third-party traffic to pass through subscribers' internet connections, using their home internet addresses and bandwidth without permission. Researchers also found collection of device, network and account information, alongside persistent remote access capabilities.

For service providers, the findings highlight a supply chain risk that may not be apparent from a device's everyday performance. A functioning streaming box can still generate unexplained traffic and undermine trust in the broadband service.

"Protecting the connected home requires visibility into threats that subscribers cannot see and should not be expected to detect," said Chris Griffiths, Chief Technology Officer at Plume. "By contributing broadband intelligence to this joint effort, we helped expose hidden supply chain risks and support coordinated action to make networks safer for service providers and their subscribers."

Complementary expertise, coordinated action

The partners contributed to the Google-led effort to disrupt X.CPE:

TrendAI™ Robert McArdle, Director of Cybercrime Research at TrendAI™ "We applaud Google's decisive action in removing this threat. Our research identified over 1.3 million devices affected by this campaign. That's millions of households and businesses completely unaware that their equipment was being used as an accessory in active criminality - whether defrauding advertisers or piggybacking on their connections to carry out other attacks via residential proxies - which would commonly include identity theft impersonating people in their region. This action by Google and research partners significantly sets back these attackers, and TrendAI research will be watching them closely if they attempt to rebuild."

HUMAN Gavin Reid, CISO at HUMAN "Compromised-device networks are sustained by profit: operators take control of devices and household connections without consent, then monetise that access through proxy services and various fraud activities. Group action, as exemplified in this operation, interrupts the infrastructure needed for monetisation, raising the cost of operating these networks and weakening the incentives that sustain them. "

SYNTHIENT Benjamin Brundage, CEO at Synthient. "Illicit pay-per-install networks provide a significant backbone to the larger fraud ecosystem, powering everything from direct ad fraud to unregulated proxy networks that push credential stuffing and DDoS botnets. The takedown of X.Cpe helps protect this space as a whole, as well as the unsuspecting consumers victimized by this scheme." - Benjamin Brundage

Title: FBI Attributes Binance Heist to North Korea’s TraderTraitor
Context: “At current prices, the attacker now controls around $3
Full Text:
North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last week, according to the FBI.

A brief statement from the Bureau published on October 31 attributed the breach to the TraderTraitor group (aka Jade Sleet, UNC4899, Slow Pisces).

“The FBI, together with partners at the US Secret Service and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH),” it read.

“It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using decentralized finance products (DeFi) and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages.”

Read more on TraderTraitor: US and Japan Blame North Korea for $308m Crypto Heist.

The FBI and its partners urged crypto entities including THORNode operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, blockchain analytics firms and other virtual asset service providers to “block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets.”

According to Blockchain analytics company Elliptic, around $2.9bn of the stolen funds have been frozen or seized, but that still leaves almost $3.3bn outside the reach of issuers.

“At current prices, the attacker now controls around $3.25bn of assets that cannot be frozen by an issuer, spread across more than 800 addresses. This includes around 584,000 ETH ($1.32bn), 18,327 BTC ($1.42bn) and 233 million XRP,” Elliptic explained.

“The ETH includes TRX laundered through bridges, which arrives on Ethereum and is split across hundreds of fresh wallets. Almost all of the stolen TRX has now been laundered. The XRP, SOL and NEAR, worth around $439m, have not moved at all since they were stolen.”

Binance Investigation Continues

Binance has said it will cover the costs of the incident, so customer funds are not in danger. However, it continues to investigate the actual cause of the breach.

Originally, the firm claimed that a compromised DevOps laptop may have been the source of the incident, but later added that it “uncovered additional points of breach” in what it is describing as a “complex attack.”

The attack was carried out by more than one individual, and used a “self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as it ran,” which has made forensic analysis harder, according to Elliptic.

TraderTraitor, which also has links to the Lazarus Group, APT 38 and AppleJeus, has been pegged for a string of historic crypto heists.

These include attacks on Japanese firm DMM, which cost the firm $308m, as well as Alphapo ($60m), CoinsPaid ($37m) and Atomic Wallet ($100m). TraderTraitor was also blamed for the previous record setter for biggest ever crypto breach, when it stole $1.5bn from Bybit.

Full Text:
Key Takeaways

CISA AA26-194A provides actionable guidance to improve the security of Internet-facing Cisco routers against real-world attack techniques.

The advisory focuses on configuration hardening and security hygiene, rather than a single vulnerability or CVE.

Manually validating advisory recommendations across enterprise networks is difficult, time-consuming, and prone to inconsistencies.

Qualys Policy Audit transforms advisory guidance into automated configuration compliance checks, enabling organizations to continuously assess Cisco router configurations.

Organizations can quickly identify configuration gaps, prioritize remediation, and continuously measure compliance using an out-of-the-box assessment policy.

Cybersecurity advisories provide valuable guidance for defending against evolving threats, but their true value lies in how quickly organizations can translate recommendations into measurable security controls. With the release of the CISA Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA26-194A, security teams now have concrete guidance to strengthen the security posture of their Internet-facing Cisco routers. With Qualys Policy Audit, organizations can automate configuration assessments to operationalize these crucial recommendations.

It is crucial to acknowledge that actors sponsored by the Russian state are actively exploiting misconfigured and vulnerable networking devices, such as Cisco routers, to penetrate enterprise and critical infrastructure networks. This access enables them to move deeper into these environments without detection. In response, CISA, the NSA, and international partners have published AA26-194A, which provides clear guidance on hardening these devices against these threats.

Organizations must understand that the guidance isn’t the hard part; the real challenge lies in ensuring that every router in production adheres to it. This is the gap where most organizations struggle. Addressing that gap requires ongoing compliance verification rather than a one-time assessment. It is important to start assessing your Cisco routers in accordance with the advisory’s recommendations.

Understanding CISA AA26-194A

CISA is committed to enhancing cybersecurity and regularly publishes periodically Joint Cybersecurity Advisories in collaboration with the National Security Agency (NSA) and other international partners. AA26-194A, titled Improve Router Hygiene to Protect Against Russian State-Sponsored Targeting, delivers crucial insights based on real-world threat intelligence, incident response findings, and observed attacker techniques.

This advisory shows that attackers exploit weak configurations, legacy management protocols, insecure administrative access, and unsupported devices to infiltrate enterprise networks.

It is crucial to implement the advisory’s recommendations, which focus on fundamental security practices. These include using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), restricting management access, disabling unnecessary services, removing insecure default configurations, maintaining updated software versions, and continuously monitoring network device configurations. Taking these steps is essential for ensuring robust network security and resilience against potential threats.

Routers are the frontline defense systems exposed to the internet, making them crucial in safeguarding enterprise networks. A single insecure configuration can enable attackers to establish persistence, intercept traffic, or move laterally within the environment.

Title: ICO Reprimands Staffordshire Police After Domestic Abuse Breach
Context: Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to...
Full Text:
A UK police force committed a serious breach of data protection law after sharing the home address of a domestic abuse victim with their abuser, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has revealed.

The privacy regulator issued a reprimand to Staffordshire Police on October 28, following the incident in March 2024.

The force had served the abuser, “P,” a Domestic Violence Protection Notice (DVPN) on their release from prison in order to protect the abuse victim, or “data subject.”

However, it erroneously included that person’s home address, which was not previously known to P.

“As a consequence of the investigation into the relevant incident the commission has become aware of allegations that P subjected the data subject to both physical and emotional abuse over a period of several years, resulting in the data subject having to relocate their home address on numerous occasions in order to escape the alleged abuse,” the reprimand noted.

“In this context, the data subject’s current address was highly sensitive information and should have been handled as such.”

Read more on police privacy breaches: Police Scotland Fined After Sharing Victim’s Phone Data.

Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to prevent the disclosure, “including poor completion rates for mandatory training in both data protection and issuing DVPNs.”

It argued that Staffordshire Police had since made improvements to reduce the risk of a similar event taking place in the future. These included increased training completion rates, new leadership roles for domestic abuse cases, new internal procedures and new technology to improve services for victims.

ICO head of investigations, Sally-Anne Poole, said the case is a reminder of the importance of getting the basics right.

“Every organization must be doing everything necessary to protect the personal information in their care, especially where there is a known risk to someone's safety,” she added. “Whether in policing, health or local government, we urge organizations to take responsibility for training their staff and putting appropriate systems in place to avoid these incidents and the harm they can cause.”

Advice for Handling Sensitive Information

The ICO warned back in 2023 that organizations handling the personally identifiable information (PII) of domestic abuse victims could put lives at risk if breaches occur.

It said at the time that it had issued reprimands to seven organizations in the previous 14 months after sensitive PII was breached, including one police force.

The latest revelations will do little to allay concerns that the regulator’s public sector approach – which favors warnings, reprimands and enforcement notices over fines – is not having the desired effect.

After this latest incident the ICO advised organizations handling sensitive PII to:

Ensure staff know how to handle the PII of people experiencing domestic abuse with extra care

Review default templates and processes to ensure PII is only included where legally necessary

Regularly check contact information to avoid disclosing information to an old address, email or phone number

Always double check before any PII is transferred, altered or disclosed

Ensure training is thorough, relevant and tailored to the tasks staff actually carry out

Title: NIST Publishes Guidance to Meet Federal Post-Quantum Deadlines
Context: For example, agencies and federal suppliers should prioritize the migration to the PQC key establishment standard (FIPS 203) for data that is particularly sensitive or needs to...
Full Text:
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has published official guidance designed to help federal government agencies meet the 2031 deadline to transition post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

President Trump’s Executive Order 14412, published in June 2026, mandated that all US federal agencies transition “high value assets” and “high impact systems” to use PQC for key establishment by December 31 2030 and for “digital signatures” by December 31 2031.

NIST’s new document sets out a transition plan for agencies and organizations that work with the federal government to meet this deadline. The guidance references the post-quantum algorithm standards that NIST published in 2024.

“These deadlines leave little margin: meeting them will require immediate and sustained action by federal agencies and by the technology providers, standards organizations, and infrastructure operators on which federal systems depend,” NIST wrote.

How to Prioritize the PQC Transition

The NIST report emphasized the logistical complexity that comes with the PQC transition. It outlined the approaches that can be taken for different types of systems and data to ensure security teams to take a risk-based approach to the transition.

For example, agencies and federal suppliers should prioritize the migration to the PQC key establishment standard (FIPS 203) for data that is particularly sensitive or needs to be kept secure for a long time, due to the risk of “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks.

The NIST guidance also accommodates a hybrid option for particularly sensitive systems, which combines conventional encryption with PQC – essentially providing two layers of security. However, this approach would demand more computational resources.

It also sets out how long less critical systems can continue to use conventional encryption protocols.

NIST mathematician Dustin Moody commented: “We lay out how certain encryption algorithms people are using today will get phased out. It’s important to know how a given algorithm might be disallowed in federal systems after a certain date, for instance, or whether it will be allowed but at the user’s own risk. Factors like this can help an organization plan.”

The report also urges federal agencies to look beyond their own system components and at its entire cryptographic supply chain.

Post-Quantum Preparations Ramp Up

The new NIST guidance follows a series of pledges around PQC transition from other governments and across the tech world.

Governments like Canada, Australia, Japan, and the UK have set deadlines ranging from 2028 to 2030 as milestones for ensuring critical government systems are quantum safe.

While many of these mandates are focused on government and critical infrastructure organizations, they generally come with a push for other sectors to follow suit and set a roadmap for PQC migration.

Large tech firms, including Cloudflare, Google and Microsoft, have set a 2029 deadline for full PQC migration. Meanwhile, Apple, AWS, IBM and Meta, have officially started rolling out NIST-approved PQC algorithms into their products.

Read now: How Cybersecurity Vendors Are Preparing for the Post-Quantum Era

The situation has been made more urgent after warnings from tech companies like Microsoft that advances in quantum R&D mean that cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs) capable of cracking asymmetric encryption could appear sooner than anticipated – potentially within the next five years.

Title: Hive ransomware affiliate jailed, years after FBI infiltrated the gang’s systems
Context: Such was the scale of the attacks that in 2022 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) described Hive as an "exceptionally aggressive" threat to the health sector
Full Text:
A Ukrainian man has been sentenced to 70 months in a US prison for his role in a series of ransomware attacks.

36-year-old Artem Stryzhak became an affiliate of the Nefilim ransomware group around June 2021, receiving an 80% cut of the ransoms he managed to extort in attacks against hospitals, government organisations, law firms, and businesses around the world.

The rest of the ransom would go to Nefilim's administrators - including fellow Ukrainian Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who was charged last year in relation to attacks against hundreds of corporate victims using the LockerGoga and MegaCortex ransomware, as well as Nefilim.

At the time of writing, Tymoshchuk is not in US custody and a US $11 million bounty has been offered by the US State Department for information leading to his arrest.

Nefilim was not the only ransomware gang that Stryzhak worked closely with. He was also an early affiliate of the Hive ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation which targeted businesses and, in particular, organisations working in healthcare.

The FBI later warned that Hive had extorted US $100 million from businesses and organisations globally in a period of just 18 months.

According to the US Department of Justice, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators were behind Hive ransomware attacks against a number of victims, including law firms, a dentist's office, and a healthcare provider, during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Such was the scale of the attacks that in 2022 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) described Hive as an "exceptionally aggressive" threat to the health sector.

In January 2023, it was revealed that a multinational law enforcement operation had secretly penetrated the Hive ransomware operation in late July 2022, capturing decryption keys and quietly passing them to victims so they did not have to pay a ransom.

The DOJ said that the operation saved corporate victims of Hive over US $130 million in ransom payments.

At the time I speculated that the take-down of Hive may lead to the identification and possible apprehension of some of those involved in Hive ransomware attacks. In June 2024, Stryzhak was arrested in Barcelona, and subsequently extradited to the United States where he pleaded guilty.

The infiltration into Hive's infrastructure took place in 2022. Stryzhak was arrested in 2024, and sentenced in 2026. If there's a lesson for ransomware affiliates who think they got away with it, it's that law enforcement is prepared to be patient, and the evidence does not go away.

That's something that Volodymyr Tymoshchuk may also want to consider.

Title: From industry concern to practical action: the value of working with regulators

Sharing cyber incident information quickly, whilst responding to an incident, is an important contributor to UK cyber resilience.

High-profile incidents in the retail sector highlighted the value of timely cyber incident information sharing, not just within the retail sector but with other sectors too. Organisations often rely on the same technologies, suppliers and digital supply chains, meaning an incident affecting one organisation or sector may expose similar vulnerabilities elsewhere. Sharing information enables organisations to learn, adapt and defend themselves against common threats before they cause further harm.

Organisations can share cyber incident information with the NCSC and through trusted information-sharing communities. However, information sharing often takes place under significant operational, legal and commercial pressures. For some organisations, questions about regulatory obligations can create hesitation at exactly the point where timely information may be most valuable to others.

Title: CISA 2030 Sets Out ‘Aggressive, Anticipatory’ Cyber Defense Strategy for Critical Infrastructure
Context: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (CISA) has promised to move away from “passive defense” and towards an “aggressive, anticipatory” approach to cyber-threats...
Full Text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (CISA) has promised to move away from “passive defense” and towards an “aggressive, anticipatory” approach to cyber-threats affecting critical infrastructure.

This was the message of CISA’s new strategy document, CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, published on October 26.

The agency provided details on how it will adopt a proactive stance when defending critical infrastructure, including responding to threats faster and building resilient systems.

Nick Anderson, acting director of CISA, wrote in the new CISA document: “The threat landscape we face today is not static. Nation-state actors and other malicious adversaries continue to grow more sophisticated in their efforts to compromise our networks, and there is no guarantee that a strong defense will eliminate intrusions.”

He added: “As President Trump has reminded us, resilience must be the foundation of our approach. We must ensure that when adversaries gain a foothold, we are prepared to detect them quickly, evict them decisively, and keep critical operations running without interruption.”

The strategy is designed to execute recent White House policy announcements around cybersecurity.

This includes the national cyber strategy published in March 2026, which outlined a broad framework for addressing cyber threats through government coordination, private sector partnerships and technological investment.

It emphasized using the full range of government capabilities, including offensive cyber operations, law enforcement measures and economic sanctions, to deter attacks and dismantle criminal networks.

In August 2026, President Trump announced that federal law enforcement agencies have been authorized to collaborate with private firms in conducting offensive cyber strikes on foreign threat actors targeting the US.

Read now: FBI Publishes First-Ever Cyber Strategy, With Focus on Disrupting Threat Actors

The CISA 2030 Three Pillar Strategy

The new CISA strategy sets out a roadmap to reach objectives across three pillars by 2030. These are:

Defend: Lead National Cyber Defense

CISA said it will integrate cyber defense capabilities of government, industry, State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT) partners, and international organizations to improve the understanding of threat activity, reduce national cyber risk and strengthen cyber defenses.

One focus area will be to work with operational technology (OT) owners and operators to modernize OT environments and enhance supply chain security.

Another will be to lead the assessment and rapid deployment of emerging technology for cybersecurity.

Harden: Prioritize National Infrastructure Security

This CISA 2030 pillar will focus on integrating intelligence across critical infrastructure security operations.

This includes targeted investment in modernized tools to enable real-time decision making and alerts, as well as accelerating operational response across the critical infrastructure community.

Intelligence will also be used to ensure CISA can prioritize its efforts and resources in the areas that have the biggest impact on national infrastructure security.

Prevail: Mobilize National Resilience

The strategy also emphasized the need to ensure resilient communications and connectivity in the face of growing cyber-attacks.

CISA said it will expand priority telecommunications services utilizing next-generation capabilities to ensure emergency connectivity.

The agency will also invest in scalable, encrypted, and resilient infrastructure that enables integrated operation, protects emergency communications, and ensures continuity of essential functions in the event of disruption.

CISA promised to deliver an approach for implementation and measurement of outcomes within 180 days, and an update on its progress against implementation within 365 days.

The European Commission has opened an investigation Booking.com for possible security failings that have resulted in fraudulent listings and phishing scams.

The investigation will ascertain whether the online travel agency has breached security and transparency provisions contained in the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA).

Among the focus areas of the investigation, the Commission will assess whether Booking.com has diligently assessed and mitigated phishing risks to customers. This includes looking at how the firm shares reservation and guest data is shared with accommodation providers, and the safeguards it has in place to prevent such data being misused to carry out phishing and solicit fraudulent payments.

In addition, the Commission will focus on the design and functioning of Booking.com's messaging service, and its potential to be abused by malicious actors for phishing attacks.

Another focus is whether the provider of Booking.com has properly assessed and mitigated the systemic risks linked to the dissemination of illegal content, such as impersonation fraud and non-compliant accommodation.

The firm’s advertising practices will also be assessed to determine whether it meets the DSA's advertising transparency obligations.

If it is determined that the company failed to comply with the DSA in these areas, Booking.com could face a fine of up to 6% of their global annual turnover and be required to take corrective measures.

The DSA came into force in November 2022 and applies to Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs).

The decision to launch formal proceedings against Booking.com, announced on October 21, follows a preliminary investigation carried out by the Commission.

Commenting on the decision, Henna Virkkunen, the Commissions’ executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The DSA sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.”

The Commission emphasized that the opening of formal proceedings does not prejudge any final outcome or decision and is empowered to accept commitments offered by Booking.com to remedy the matters subject to the proceedings.

Booking.com Customers a Frequent Target for Phishing Attacks

Numerous phishing campaigns targeting Booking.com customers and partners have been observed by cybersecurity researchers in recent years. These campaigns have included threat actors accessing the personal details of Booking.com customers and spoofing the company’s email domains to send malicious messages.

In 2023, Secureworks, now part of Sophos, reported how cybercriminals deployed the Vidar infostealer to gain access partner hotels’ Booking.com credentials. This information was then used to send phishing emails to Booking.com customers and trick them into handing over their payment details, in many cases leading to money being stolen.

Microsoft reported a ClickFix campaign that impersonated Booking.com in March 2025. This began with the threat actor sending malicious email impersonating Booking.com to targeted individuals in North America, Oceania, South and Southeast Asia and Europe. The attack attempted to lure these individuals into downloading infostealer malware.

In June 2026, TrendAI Research identified a phishing campaign targeting Booking.com partner accommodations in Japan. These emails impersonated guest complaints and review requests to trick hotel staff into executing malicious files.

Title: Localizing compliance at scale: Achieving South Korea’s ISMS certification
Context: We document the limits of IP geolocation: it is an estimate rather than an exact science, addresses rotate and change ownership, and it should not be the only signal where the...
Full Text:
For ten days, auditors appointed by the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) sat together with us and worked through 80 controls. That is what it took for a company headquartered in the United States, operating a global network serving Korean users, to be certified in South Korea. Cloudflare has now obtained South Korea's Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification under the ISMS-P framework.

For customers in Korea, this is more than a compliance checkbox. It is evidence that Cloudflare's security and privacy program has been examined not only for whether our controls exist, but for how they operate in the context of Korean law, the Korean language, and the particular expectations of Korean regulators.

What a Korean user sees when they sign up

The most visible result of this work is the Cloudflare account sign-up page. In most parts of the world, the line that sits above the sign-up button reads: "By continuing, I agree to Cloudflare's terms, privacy policy, and cookie policy."

A user signing up from South Korea sees something different. The Korean experience is triggered by the country selected at sign-up and by IP geolocation from within South Korea, and it breaks the same agreement into four separately labeled items, each marked required or optional, each linking to its full text, with an option to agree to all of them at once:

모두 동의 (Agree to all)

[필수] 서비스 약관 ([Required] Terms of Service)

[필수] 개인정보 수집 및 이용 ([Required] Collection and use of personal information)

[필수] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 해외 이전 ([Required] Transfer of a limited amount of personal information overseas)

[선택] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 제3자 제공 ([Optional] Sharing a limited amount of personal information with marketing third parties)

The three required items are hard gates. The sign-up button stays disabled until all three are checked, so there is no path through the form that creates an account without an affirmative action on each one. The optional item governs marketing permission only, and leaving it unchecked has no effect on the account creation (it merely opts the user out of receiving marketing communications).

The hard part: sign-up paths that never show a form

Itemizing consent on a form we control is straightforward. The difficulty was the sign-up paths that skip that form entirely.

Globally, you can create a Cloudflare account with Google, Apple, or GitHub. Those flows hand the user to an identity provider and return with an authenticated identity, and they never render our own sign-up form, which is precisely where the four consent items live. There is no step in that handoff where we can present three required items, link each to its full Korean text, and require an affirmative action on each before the account exists. The identity provider's screen is not ours to change.

We could either build a separate post-authentication consent gate for one country, or remove the paths that bypass the gate we already had. We chose the second. Social sign-up is not offered in South Korea, so every account created there goes through Cloudflare’s sign-up form, which enforces the required consents.

The country signal is the same one available to any Cloudflare customer. Cloudflare derives a two-letter country code from the client IP address and exposes it on the request, as the CF-IPCountry header at the origin and as request.cf.country inside a Worker. Reduced to its essentials, the branch is a string comparison:

// Illustrative: the shape of the check, not Cloudflare's own dashboard code. export default { async fetch(request) { // Two-letter country code derived from the client IP. // Same value as the CF-IPCountry request header. // Cloudflare's network populates this on the incoming request, so there is // no geolocation database, lookup service, or extra round trip of our own. const country = request.cf?.country; if (country === "KR") { return renderSignUp({ locale: "ko-KR", consent: "itemized", // four separate items, three of them required socialLogin: false, // no path that skips the consent form }); } return renderSignUp({ locale: "en-US", consent: "combined", socialLogin: true }); }, };

What that does not show is why the country code is not the whole trigger. We document the limits of IP geolocation: it is an estimate rather than an exact science, addresses rotate and change ownership, and it should not be the only signal where the use case is critical to meeting the objectives of a local requirement. A Korean resident traveling abroad, or behind a VPN or a mobile carrier's NAT, may not arrive with a Korean address. So IP-based geolocation decides which form appears by default, but the country a user selects at sign-up overrides that and carries the decision from there. The IP address tells us where a request came from; only the user can tell us where they reside. Keeping those two apart is what makes the consent meaningful rather than presumed.

It is a small feature. It took a country-level product decision, and a change to the account creation path.

What ISMS is and why it matters

ISMS is a detailed, localized certification standard. It covers security policy, access control, authentication and permission management, encryption, incident response, risk management, and disaster recovery, all assessed against how personal data actually moves through an organization's systems, and against Korea's Personal Information Protection Act and its associated regulatory guidelines.

Certification requires an independent audit by an auditor appointed by KISA, a governmental institution affiliated with the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), followed by review from a special committee. It is valid for three years, with an annual audit required to maintain it.

The ISMS certification is primarily established under Article 47 of Korea's Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc., with the certification criteria and procedure set out in its Enforcement Decree and in the public notification on ISMS certification issued by MSIT.

What the audit examined

Cloudflare is already certified against ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018 and many other globally recognized frameworks. ISMS does not replace any of them. It is a localization of the same principles, layered with Korean regulatory requirements, and that changes what auditors look for and how they look for it.

The controls in scope started with the review of data flows. We presented detailed data flow diagrams showing every path by which employees could access personal information that Cloudflare collects, processes, and stores. The flows themselves are not Korea-specific. What was different was the form the evidence had to take: the auditors were not willing to work from a narrative description of how data moves, they wanted diagrams they could read and interrogate. For each one, they examined every access control layer and tested its effectiveness, across our internal systems, our public-facing websites, event pages, and the Cloudflare dashboard, covering the full lifecycle of a user's data from first interaction through to destruction. Those diagrams are not published here due to confidentiality.

The audit also scrutinized the language and terminology of our consent collection: the exact wording at sign-up, the structure of each notification, and whether the items were presented separately and clearly. That is the kind of detail the ISMS framework is designed to surface.

Why the timeline ran to a year and a half

Part of the answer is how audit cycles work. An ISMS audit covers a single annual period, and all evidence, documentation, and systems must reflect that period. Our preparation ran past one audit year and into the next, which meant retranslating updated policies for the new audit year, re-collecting and reassessing evidence, republishing an updated privacy policy, and absorbing formatting and design changes our marketing and website teams had introduced in the meantime.

What the certificate covers

KISA defines the certified scope as a service boundary rather than as an enumerated list of in-scope products. The Statement of Scope submitted to KISA describes that boundary in three parts:

the organizational and operational perimeter: the Cloudflare entities, teams, and processes that operate the service;

the infrastructure perimeter: the network and platform the certified service runs on;

the information assets and personal information flows that fall inside the boundary under the ISMS control set.

If a customer-consumed Cloudflare product is delivered through that certified service boundary, meaning it runs on the same certified platform, is operated by the same certified teams, and is governed by the same ISMS, it is covered by the certificate. The certificate is held by Cloudflare, Inc.

That is a different shape from the reports most procurement teams work with. A SOC 2 report or an ISO 27001 certificate describes the system it covers and names the services included, so coverage is confirmed by finding the product in that list. The ISMS certificate carries no such list. Coverage follows the delivery path instead, whether or not a product is named anywhere.

What this means for customers

For organizations operating in Korea, this gives legal, security, and procurement teams a local assurance benchmark alongside Cloudflare's broader compliance portfolio. ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 demonstrate a general security posture. ISMS reflects Korea-specific legal and regulatory expectations. That distinction matters in third-party risk reviews and in preparing for a team’s own compliance assessments.

Cloudflare’s entry can be found on KISA's public register of certified organizations, which is the independent, verifiable confirmation to cite in a risk review. Broader privacy and data protection material sits on the Cloudflare Trust Hub.

The question that usually stalls a vendor review of Cloudflare is whether a particular product in use is in scope. The certificate does not answer that by name, because it lists no products. It answers by boundary, meaning that the product is in scope if it is delivered through the certified service.

For multinational teams managing security across regions, the certification confirms that Cloudflare's program has been reviewed against local requirements in one of Asia's most important digital markets, not just designed for global scale.

Building a better Internet, for everyone

ISMS is not a harder certification than the other assurance audits we go through. It is a more nuanced one. It is built around the regulatory needs of one specific region, and it asks for genuine investment in understanding and embedding those needs, rather than mapping them onto a common control framework.

Going through it made Cloudflare more global, not less. It pushed us to think carefully about what it means to serve users in a specific local context, with local language, local consent expectations, and local data protection requirements, and to put that into how the product behaves rather than only into a document.

That is consistent with what we are working toward: helping build a better Internet for everyone, not just in the regions where regulatory requirements are straightforward, but everywhere.

To learn more about Cloudflare's compliance and assurance programs, visit our Trust Hub.

Sonatype is responding to the industry-wide eMudhra certificate authority incident, which affects certificate trust stores used by certain Sonatype products and distributions. We are updating affected components. In the meantime, apply certificate trust-store updates provided by your operating-system, runtime, and application vendors.

What Happened

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) could be recovered because they were generated with insufficient randomness. Six affected intermediates were for TLS certificates and two were for code signing. Someone with an affected TLS key could create a certificate for a website or service, which could be accepted by clients that still trust the affected chain.

Browser and operating system vendors have taken steps to block the affected certificates. Other software may rely on separate or bundled certificate trust stores that need updates, so organizations should also check systems beyond browsers and operating systems.

We are preparing updated Docker images and patch releases with current certificate trust data. The tables below list the impacted Sonatype products and their remediation status. Existing Docker images and bundled JVMs do not update automatically.
